chunks.title: Top Generative AI Service Providers 2026: Penetration Maturity (PeMa) Quadrant
chunks.text: Top Generative AI Service Providers 2026: Penetration Maturity (PeMa) Quadrant. Published by AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC) (2026-04). Type: report. Method: Vendor study. 28 GenAI service providers took part voluntarily through a questionnaire, briefing calls and supporting case material, complemented by secondary research. Each vendor is scored on two normalised 0 to 1 indices, Penetration (market reach) and Maturity (technical and delivery depth), and placed in one of four quadrants. Sample: 28 participating vendors. Sponsor: none. How we use it: Market findings, delivery challenges, service taxonomy, pricing and engagement benchmarks, and the 28-vendor landscape with scores and quadrant placement. Caveats: Vendor-submitted data is not independently audited by the publisher. Vendors that disclose performance figures (such as POC-to-production rates) tend to be the strong performers, so disclosed metrics are selectively reported.

chunks.title: 2026 State of Real-Time Data: Agentic Enterprises Are Running on Real-Time Data
chunks.text: 2026 State of Real-Time Data: Agentic Enterprises Are Running on Real-Time Data. Published by IDC Custom Solutions (2026-09). Type: survey. Method: Custom survey (IDC Real-Time Data Study) fielded in June 2026. Respondents were scored 0 to 100 on real-time data maturity, blending real-time deployment depth, agentic AI adoption and measurable outcomes, then split into four percentile tiers. Sample: 623 senior technology decision-makers at enterprises with revenue above 1 billion USD, across eight countries, led by manufacturing, financial services and retail. 78 percent are primary decision-makers for real-time data; 71 percent own AI or agentic initiatives.. Sponsor: Solace. How we use it: Buyer-side adoption statistics, maturity-tier comparisons, barriers to scaling agents, technical challenges, and what leading organisations do differently. Caveats: Sponsored by Solace, a real-time data platform vendor. The brief's framing (real-time data as the deciding factor for agentic success) aligns with the sponsor's product. The maturity score itself includes real-time deployment as an input, so part of the correlation between maturity and real-time adoption is built in. We report the survey numbers as measured and flag this framing.

chunks.title: The State of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI
chunks.text: The State of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI. Published by McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack) (2026-08). Type: survey. Method: Annual online global survey fielded 4 May to 8 June 2026, with 1,719 participants across 97 countries, industries, company sizes and functions. Sample: 1,719 respondents. Sponsor: none. How we use it: Global adoption and scaling rates, agent deployment by function, EBIT impact, high-performer traits, and year-over-year trend. Caveats: Self-reported survey of executives; McKinsey also sells AI consulting services. Weighting and respondent mix are as described in the report.

chunks.title: State of AI in the Enterprise: The untapped edge (2026 report)
chunks.text: State of AI in the Enterprise: The untapped edge (2026 report). Published by Deloitte AI Institute (2026-01). Type: survey. Method: Global survey of 3,235 senior leaders (board, C-suite, president, VP and director level), fielded August to September 2025, split equally between IT and line-of-business leaders across 24 countries. Sample: 3,235 senior leaders, 24 countries. Sponsor: none. How we use it: Value realised by type, depth of transformation, barriers (skills, governance), agentic AI potential by function, and governance-value link. Caveats: Self-reported survey; Deloitte sells AI advisory services. Fielded in late 2025, so it predates the 2026 sources by several months.

chunks.title: BCG AI Radar 2026: As AI Investments Surge, CEOs Take the Lead
chunks.text: BCG AI Radar 2026: As AI Investments Surge, CEOs Take the Lead. Published by Boston Consulting Group (2026-01). Type: survey. Method: Survey of 2,360 executives, including 640 CEOs, across 16 markets and nine industries. Sample: 2,360 executives incl. 640 CEOs. Sponsor: none. How we use it: AI investment as a share of revenue, CEO ownership of AI decisions, the value gap, investment resilience, and value-driver breakdown. Caveats: Self-reported survey; BCG sells AI consulting services.

chunks.title: The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025
chunks.text: The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025. Published by MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab) (2025-07). Type: report. Method: Multi-method study, January to June 2025: systematic review of more than 300 publicly disclosed AI initiatives, 52 structured interviews, and 153 survey responses from senior leaders gathered at four conferences. Sample: 300+ deployments, 52 interviews, 153 survey responses. Sponsor: none. How we use it: The pilot-to-production 'divide', reasons pilots stall (lack of learning and context), buy-versus-build outcomes, and shadow AI usage. Caveats: Small and convenience-based survey sample; the headline 95 percent figure has been widely quoted and debated. Preliminary version (v0.1) of the report. Predates the 2026 sources by a year.

chunks.title: 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise
chunks.text: 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise. Published by Menlo Ventures (2025-12). Type: web. Method: Survey of about 495 US enterprise AI decision-makers, fielded 7 to 25 November 2025, combined with Menlo's own market sizing. Sample: About 495 US enterprise decision-makers. Sponsor: none. How we use it: Enterprise GenAI spend and growth, spend by layer and department, buy-versus-build split, and vendor share shifts. Caveats: Published by a venture capital firm with investments in AI companies; market-share figures are estimates.

chunks.title: Leaders, gainers and unexpected winners in the enterprise AI arms race (third annual CIO survey)
chunks.text: Leaders, gainers and unexpected winners in the enterprise AI arms race (third annual CIO survey). Published by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) (2026-01). Type: web. Method: Third-party survey of 100 VPs and C-level executives at Global 2000 companies (88 percent above 1 billion USD revenue), run through an independent expert network, published 30 January 2026. Sample: 100 Global 2000 executives. Sponsor: none. How we use it: Enterprise AI budget per company and growth, multi-model strategies, buy-versus-build, and application adoption. Caveats: Published by a venture capital firm with investments in AI companies. Small sample.

chunks.title: AI Quarterly Pulse Survey, Q2 2026
chunks.text: AI Quarterly Pulse Survey, Q2 2026. Published by KPMG US (2026-06). Type: survey. Method: Quarterly survey of 204 US C-suite and business leaders at organisations with annual revenue of 1 billion USD or more, fielded 28 April to 25 May 2026. Sample: 204 US leaders at $1B+ firms. Sponsor: none. How we use it: Most recent agent deployment and scaling rates, employee adoption of agents, and the shift toward cost visibility and governance. Caveats: Small US-only sample; KPMG sells AI advisory services. Quarter-over-quarter comparisons rely on separate samples.

chunks.title: 2026 Work Trend Index Annual Report
chunks.text: 2026 Work Trend Index Annual Report. Published by Microsoft (2026-05). Type: report. Method: Survey of 20,000 workers using AI across 10 countries, combined with anonymised Microsoft 365 productivity signals and analysis of more than 100,000 Copilot conversations. Sample: 20,000 workers, 10 countries. Sponsor: Microsoft. How we use it: Workforce-side adoption, the organisational readiness gap, and how work is being redesigned around agents. Caveats: Vendor-published research from a company selling AI products; usage signals come from its own platform. Treated like the Solace-sponsored IDC brief.

chunks.title: Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2026
chunks.text: Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2026. Published by Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI) (2026-04). Type: report. Method: Annual compilation of indicators from academic, industry and government sources across nine chapters. We use the Economy and Public Opinion chapters only. Sample: Compiled indicators; underlying surveys vary by indicator. Sponsor: none. How we use it: Organisational adoption rates, corporate investment, productivity evidence, and public opinion on AI. Caveats: Academic and broadly neutral. Many of its business indicators are themselves drawn from surveys by McKinsey and others, so it is not fully independent of src-03.

chunks.title: FutureScape 2026: Moving into the agentic future (public summary)
chunks.text: FutureScape 2026: Moving into the agentic future (public summary). Published by IDC (2025-10). Type: web. Method: Public blog summary of IDC's FutureScape 2026 predictions (35 prediction sets across 12 industries). The full prediction documents are for IDC subscribers and were not used. Sample: Analyst predictions. Sponsor: none. How we use it: Forward-looking predictions on agentic AI adoption and spending, used in the outlook section only. Caveats: Summary-only source with lower evidence weight. Predictions, not measurements.

chunks.title: The question has moved from what GenAI can do to who can run it in production
chunks.text: Buyers no longer ask what is possible. They ask which providers can turn pilots into governed systems inside core workflows, and why their last pilots did not get there. The AIM vendor study frames the 2026 market around a single buyer question: which providers can take a pilot all the way to a governed production system that lives inside day-to-day business processes. IDC's buyer survey shows the same shift from the demand side, describing agentic AI as an operational dependency rather than an experiment. AIM adds that when pilots stall, the model is seldom the culprit, and in most cases the blocker is the data, operations, governance or organisation around it. Deloitte's 2026 report, based on a survey of 3,235 leaders, likewise finds that pilots stall mainly on the extra work production demands, such as integration, security review, compliance and monitoring, though it notes that a model that did well in testing can still fall short at scale. BCG shows the question now has an owner: 72% of CEOs call themselves the main AI decision-maker. Theme: Market state. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Typical POC-to-production conversion rate across vendors; Adoption attitudes toward real-time data and agentic AI; Organisations that have moved 40% or more of AI experiments into production. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 6, 8; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 4; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 7, 8, 9; Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 11.

chunks.title: Agentic AI is mainstream in intent but not yet in scaled production
chunks.text: Four in five enterprises are investing in or have deployed agentic AI, yet only a minority run several agents in production, and vendors confirm scaled agentic work is still a small share of engagements. IDC finds 80 percent of large enterprises investing in or already deploying agentic AI. But the share with several agents in production ranges from 20 percent among the least mature to 59 percent among Leaders, and roughly half of the two lower tiers are still in the investing stage. AIM's vendor view agrees: agentic AI has become an active delivery priority and multi-agent platforms are launching, but agentic work that has actually reached scaled production is still a thin slice of what vendors deliver, and many of the agent references are aspirations rather than live systems. Other sources confirm the gap between intent and scaled production. Deloitte's respondents expect the share of companies using agentic AI at least moderately to rise from 23% to 74% within two years, and McKinsey found about one in five scaling agents in mid-2026. Menlo classes 16% of enterprise deployments as true agents, and a16z finds 13% of its respondents running agentic workflow automation in production. Theme: Agentic AI. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Adoption attitudes toward real-time data and agentic AI; Organisations with several AI agents already in production, by maturity tier; Organisations investing significantly in agentic AI but not yet deployed, by tier; Organisations using agentic AI at least moderately; Extent of AI agent use by company size, 2025 vs 2026; Deployments that qualify as true agentic systems; AI use cases in production among Global 2000 respondents. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 4, 5; AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 6, 15; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 17; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 6, 7; Menlo Ventures, 2025; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: Agentic AI is the top driver of demand for real-time data
chunks.text: Advances in agentic AI are the most cited reason enterprises need faster data, ahead of security, cost and regulation. In IDC's survey, 43 percent name advances in agentic AI capability as a significant driver of increased need for real-time data. Security and AI trust requirements follow at 40 percent, cost and scalability at 38, regulatory pressure at 35 and industry disruption at 29. The reading is that agents, which must sense and act on current state, are resetting expectations for data freshness. Note that the survey sponsor sells a real-time data platform. Theme: Data foundations. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Most significant drivers of increased need for real-time data. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 6, 27.

chunks.title: Capability breadth is commoditised; differentiation is now operational
chunks.text: Nearly every provider tells the same six-stage lifecycle story. What separates them is whether they can show live production systems, how deep their accelerators go, how much domain knowledge is built in, and whether their operations hold up over time. AIM observes that vendors have converged on an identical end-to-end story: advisory at the front, then data groundwork, model work, application build, operations and an ongoing managed service. Because everyone claims the full lifecycle, breadth no longer differentiates. Buyers are shifting procurement scrutiny from what a vendor can build to what it has operated. Vendors that list dozens of POCs without production evidence are increasingly exposed. Theme: Market state. Evidence: single-source. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6, 7.

chunks.title: Most pilots fail and most vendors convert fewer than half
chunks.text: Industry pilot failure is reported above 70 percent, and most service providers convert only 25 to 45 percent of proofs of concept into production. AIM describes the POC-to-production gap as the market's defining fault line and the primary delivery bottleneck. The small set of providers that have reorganised delivery around this gap share three traits: methods aimed at the human reasons projects stall (trust, skills, resistance to new ways of working); development steered by continuous evaluation, with automated quality gates throughout the build; and named production systems with quantified outcomes. Higher performers also front-load value-case validation and structured discovery, surfacing data, governance and organisational constraints before build begins. MIT NANDA's interview sample reports about 5% of custom task-specific tools reaching sustained impact within six months, and Deloitte finds only a quarter of firms with 40% or more of experiments in production. The failure rate depends on what is counted, but every source that measures it finds most pilots do not make it. Theme: Adoption and production. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Typical POC-to-production conversion rate across vendors; Industry-wide GenAI pilot failure rate; Vendor-disclosed POC-to-production conversion rates; Adoption funnel, embedded or task-specific GenAI tools; Organisations that have moved 40% or more of AI experiments into production. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 6, 9; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 6, 7, 24; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 8.

chunks.title: Data quality is the number one problem from both the buyer and the vendor side
chunks.text: Two independent methods converge: IDC's buyers rank data quality and consistency as their top technical challenge for real-time data initiatives, and AIM's vendors call data readiness the most cited challenge and the root cause of most production failures. In the IDC survey, 46 percent cite data quality and consistency as a top technical challenge for their real-time data initiatives over the next 12 to 18 months, and it leads even among the most mature organisations. AIM finds that enterprise data is scattered across systems, formatted every which way, thinly documented and missing the context a language model needs, and that these problems surface only when moving from sanitised pilot samples to real production data. AIM sees the distance between having data and having it ready for retrieval as the biggest technical obstacle of all. Effective providers front-load data readiness assessment and treat the data groundwork as something to finish first, not something to run alongside the build. KPMG's large US firms rank data readiness the top agent barrier at 58%. MIT NANDA offers a contrasting reading: its interviewees put tools that do not learn or fit into workflows ahead of data as the main brake on adoption. Theme: Data foundations. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Top technical challenges for real-time data, next 12 to 18 months; Biggest challenges to deploying AI agents; Why users will not trust generic tools with core workflows (approximate). Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 13; AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 9; KPMG US, 2026, pages 6; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 13.

chunks.title: The hard part of agents is connecting them to data, not building them
chunks.text: Connecting agents to real-time enterprise data and managing them across frameworks tie as the top barriers to scaling agents. Ease of building agents ranks last. IDC asked which issues are top barriers to scaling AI agents. Connecting agents to real-time enterprise data and managing agents across different frameworks each score 40 percent, followed by monitoring performance and accuracy at 37, getting agents to work together at 35, human-in-the-loop oversight at 33 and LLM cost concerns at 28. Ease of building agents is cited by only 26 percent. The picture is that tooling for building agents has matured faster than the plumbing, governance and observability needed to run many of them on live enterprise context. KPMG's mid-2026 pulse confirms it from a US sample: data readiness leads the barriers at 58% while agentic complexity and technical skills trail. Theme: Agentic AI. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Top barriers to scaling AI agents; Biggest challenges to deploying AI agents. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 12; KPMG US, 2026, pages 6.

chunks.title: The production gap is organisational more than technical
chunks.text: AIM finds that lost executive sponsorship, legal intervention and user resistance sink more projects than model performance, with late compliance objections among the wider organisational barriers. AIM ranks the POC-to-production gap as the highest-impact challenge because it gates all downstream value, and states that the primary barrier is organisational readiness rather than technical capability: governance gaps, talent shortages, change-management failure and late-stage compliance objections. IDC's barrier list shows a related pattern, that running agents worries firms more than building them: connecting agents to data, managing them across frameworks, monitoring them, getting them to work together and human oversight all rank above the ease of building an agent (26%). Vendors reporting better conversion embed production planning from engagement start instead of leaving it to the deployment stage. Deloitte's diagnosis of the pilot trap lists integration, security review, compliance and monitoring as the production requirements pilots avoid. Microsoft's driver analysis finds organisational conditions about twice as strongly associated with workers' self-reported AI impact as individual ones (67% vs 32%), an association rather than a proven cause. Theme: Adoption and production. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Top barriers to scaling AI agents; Typical POC-to-production conversion rate across vendors; Organisations that have moved 40% or more of AI experiments into production; Relative importance of factors explaining reported AI impact. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 9; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 12; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 9; Microsoft, 2026, pages 16, 17.

chunks.title: Hallucination erodes trust most, and it gets worse in production
chunks.text: Edge cases and domain nuance expose model weaknesses that controlled pilots mask. Responses converge on RAG-first design, citation enforcement, confidence scoring and human review. AIM names hallucination and output reliability as the problem that does the most damage to buyer confidence and keeps GenAI out of regulated processes. Vendor responses converge on retrieval-grounded architectures, mandatory citations, confidence scores that route low-confidence answers to people, and a person checking the answer before it is used. A smaller group has gone further with continuous evaluation against ground-truth benchmarks as a standing production safeguard rather than one-time testing. Some vendors add critic or validator agents, or deterministic rule layers, on top of LLM reasoning for audit-sensitive workflows. Theme: Governance and trust. Evidence: single-source. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 9, 12, 33, 34, 42, 56.

chunks.title: Adoption, not technology, is the primary ROI risk and it is under-invested
chunks.text: Organisations spend heavily on AI technology and little on how people interact with and trust it. Vendors that treat adoption failure as the main risk produce more durable deployments. AIM finds change management and adoption design broadly under-invested across the market. Too few vendors recognise that a system that works and a system people actually use are two different achievements. Effective responses put GenAI inside the tools and processes people already use instead of standing up a separate system, train each role for its own tasks, and introduce human oversight in stages so that trust grows with experience. One vendor in the study reports that redesigning outputs and interaction around behavioural insight raised adoption by 70 to 80 percent in an insurance deployment whose model was already technically sound. Three other 2026 sources point the same way: Deloitte finds daily use flat despite wider access and skills the top barrier, Microsoft finds organisational culture the strongest predictor of AI impact, and BCG's Trailblazer CEOs devote about 60% of AI budget to upskilling. Theme: Talent and organisation. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Workers with access who use AI in their daily workflow; Talent strategy adjustments made because of AI; Relative importance of factors explaining reported AI impact; Share of AI budget going to upskilling and retraining, by CEO archetype. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 7, 9, 54; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 8, 14; Microsoft, 2026, pages 16; Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 26.

chunks.title: Costs escalate sharply from pilot to production, though buyers rank cost below other barriers
chunks.text: Pilot token costs in the hundreds of dollars can become tens of thousands at production volume. The most mature vendors treat cost as a design-time architectural decision; buyers rank LLM cost sixth of seven agent-scaling barriers. AIM places cost management and economic viability among the top five delivery challenges and lists the standard mitigations: sending each request to the cheapest model that can handle it, caching, shortening prompts and watching spend as it happens, all settled at design time rather than after deployment. Several providers now productise cost control as gateways, FinOps dashboards or tiered model architectures that send high-volume tasks to small models. On the buyer side, IDC finds LLM cost concern cited by 28 percent as a top barrier, well behind data connectivity. A plausible reading is that vendors feel the cost pressure first, or that many buyers have not yet reached production-scale token bills. By mid-2026 the cost pressure had become measurable: McKinsey finds 20% of respondents at AI-using organisations saying operating costs have led them to limit AI use, and KPMG finds only 26% with full cost visibility. Theme: Cost. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Top barriers to scaling AI agents; Organisations that have constrained AI use because of operating costs including tokens, by industry; AI use constrained by operating cost, by tool, high performers vs others; Organisations whose AI operating costs are fully visible today. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 10, 20, 50, 53, 59, 83; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 12; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 15, 22; KPMG US, 2026, pages 5.

chunks.title: GenAI, agents and classical ML are converging into integrated operational systems
chunks.text: Early GenAI was additive: RAG on data platforms, chatbots on portals. The emerging pattern is agents using LLMs as reasoning engines over tools, data and traditional models, with multi-agent orchestration as the design pattern for complex automation. AIM calls this convergence the most consequential architectural shift in the market. Agents break a task into steps, call tools, check their own results and set off follow-on actions in other enterprise systems. For complex workflow automation the pattern gaining ground is several specialised agents coordinated together, though production examples are still a minority. At least one provider explicitly fuses language models with classical ML, using the LLM as a reasoning and orchestration layer over its statistical models to gain adaptability and explainability. Theme: Agentic AI. Evidence: single-source. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6, 72.

chunks.title: RAG is table stakes; the edge is in retrieval quality, knowledge graphs and agentic RAG
chunks.text: Basic retrieval-augmented generation no longer differentiates. Differences show up in how documents are split for a given domain, whether retrieval quality is measured at scale, whether a knowledge graph backs the retrieval, and whether agents can drive it. AIM treats RAG as a baseline capability and finds enterprise knowledge retrieval the dominant workload today. The strongest implementations span dozens of catalogues, hundreds of schemas and multiple languages within a unified reasoning platform, and measuring retrieval quality at scale is one of the things that set vendors apart. Knowledge graphs, ontology layers and semantic context layers appear across many vendor profiles as the means to ground agents and reduce hallucination. The next step is retrieval run by agents, which decide on the fly what to look up, how to reason over it and what to do next. Menlo's production data show how common basic RAG is: prompt design and RAG together make up over 70% of enterprise customisation approaches, against 12% for fine-tuning and 6% for tool calling. Theme: Data foundations. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Customisation approach used in production, enterprises vs startups. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6, 12, 15, 37, 38, 53, 61, 62; Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Knowledge retrieval dominates, content generation's share is falling, autonomous execution is growing fastest
chunks.text: The mix of GenAI work is shifting from generate-text use cases toward data-grounded retrieval and multi-step agents. AIM groups vendor work into five workloads. Enterprise knowledge retrieval over internal documents and data is where most production deployments sit and the pattern enterprises adopt first. Content generation, where most organisations started, is a declining share as novelty fades. The fastest growth is in agents that carry out multi-step tasks on their own, and vendors with their own agent platforms report it approaching or exceeding half their portfolio, though the label is applied loosely by some. Domain model adaptation and multimodal processing remain selective, used where accuracy or cross-format reasoning is critical. Theme: Market state. Evidence: single-source. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 15.

chunks.title: The services market is splitting three ways: domain depth, owned platforms and operating maturity
chunks.text: Domain specialists with encoded regulatory and workflow knowledge, and platform-led vendors with individually named components, are building positions that generic providers cannot easily copy. AIM describes three fault lines. Vendors whose prebuilt solutions carry an industry's workflows, its regulations and ready-made compliance patterns hold defensible positions. Platform-led vendors whose accelerators have specific names and specific engineering jobs show materially higher productisation maturity than those with generic capability labels. Operational maturity in LLMOps and governance is the third axis. The analyst test for an accelerator: if its description would fit any vendor, it confers little advantage. Theme: Vendor landscape. Evidence: single-source. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 7.

chunks.title: Accelerator counts are high, but integrated platforms are still early
chunks.text: Every vendor discloses several proprietary accelerators, commonly between five and ten. Most are point solutions, and full platform adoption is a small share of engagements across the market; even one Leader puts it at only 10 to 15 percent. AIM notes that vendors list many accelerators, but few have yet pulled them together into a platform that clients adopt whole. Platform adoption rates sit in the early percentages of total engagements and multi-cloud support for flagship platforms is often still on the roadmap. One Leader reports component-level adoption in 70 to 80 percent of engagements but full platform deployment in only 10 to 15 percent. Buyers are advised to ask which accelerators have run in production for clients versus internal tools repackaged as client-ready. Theme: Vendor landscape. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Proprietary accelerators disclosed per vendor (typical). Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 28, 54.

chunks.title: Operations and governance decide whether GenAI holds up in production
chunks.text: Vendors that treat operations as a managed discipline with reliability engineering and cost controls, and buyers that treat governance as an accelerator, are the ones getting to scale. AIM treats LLMOps and governance as the layer that settles whether a system survives once it is live, and finds that the strongest vendors run it as an ongoing operation, with site-reliability practices and spend controls, instead of treating it as a choice of tools. IDC's recommendations to buyers include reframing governance as an accelerator rather than a brake, noting it is already a top investment priority; security and AI trust requirements are the second-ranked driver of real-time data demand. Six practice areas recur across vendors: cost and compute, token efficiency, monitoring, governance and risk, security and compliance, and value tracking. Deloitte and KPMG add the agent-era version: one in five has mature agent governance, and 52 percent name human checks on outputs, rather than oversight of each agent action, as their main way to manage agent risk over the next 6 to 12 months. Theme: Operations and LLMOps. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Most significant drivers of increased need for real-time data; Top technical challenges for real-time data, next 12 to 18 months; Organisations with a mature governance model for autonomous agents; Top planned risk control for AI agents is output-level human-in-the-loop validation. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 7, 20; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 6, 13, 22; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 20, 21; KPMG US, 2026, pages 4.

chunks.title: Leaders differ from the rest in execution, not belief
chunks.text: Three quarters or more of every maturity tier agree agents need live data, yet Leaders are far ahead in execution: about three quarters have real-time data across all workflows and seven in ten run a single unified platform, against fewer than one in ten Emerging organisations. Across IDC's tiers, agreement with its three statements about what agents need runs from 69 to 93 percent and rises with maturity; even the least mature tier agrees at 75 percent that agents need up-to-date data. Execution measures diverge sharply: real-time data across all workflows rises from 7 percent among Emerging organisations to 76 percent among Leaders, a single unified platform from 8 to 71 percent, and automating half or more of real-time processes from 23 to 91 percent. IDC summarises it as belief being universal while execution is not. McKinsey's high performers and Microsoft's Frontier Professionals also stand apart on practices such as workflow redesign, quality standards and impact measurement; neither source compares beliefs, and McKinsey's widest gap is in ambition, with high performers far more likely to expect transformative change. Theme: Adoption and production. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Agree that agents need up-to-date, accurate real-time data, by tier; Real-time data implemented across all workflows, by tier; Automating half or more of real-time processes, by tier; Run a single unified real-time data platform, by tier; Practices of AI high performers vs others (approximate); Team practices reported by Frontier vs other AI users. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 11, 14, 15; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 19; Microsoft, 2026, pages 16, 17.

chunks.title: A unified data platform is the clearest marker of a leader; tool sprawl is the enemy
chunks.text: Seven in ten Leaders run a single unified real-time data platform versus fewer than one in ten Emerging organisations. Even so, only about a third of Leaders (36 percent) report their technologies fully integrated. IDC calls the dividing line architectural. Leaders have moved onto one integrated platform, whereas most organisations still run a patchwork of weakly linked tools that they themselves say needs repair. Tool sprawl and platform complexity is a top-five technical challenge at 37 percent, alongside legacy systems and technical debt at 38. Full integration remains rare everywhere: 36 percent of Leaders and 10 percent of Emerging organisations. Consolidation is IDC's second of five recommendations. Theme: Data foundations. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Run a single unified real-time data platform, by tier; Real-time technologies fully integrated, by tier; Top technical challenges for real-time data, next 12 to 18 months. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 13, 15, 22.

chunks.title: Maturity pays: Leaders are more than three times as likely to deliver outcomes on most of their AI projects
chunks.text: 89 percent of Leaders deliver measurable outcomes on at least half their AI projects, against 26 percent of Emerging organisations. Agentic success rates roughly double across the tiers. IDC's outcome measures climb steadily with maturity. The share delivering measurable outcomes on half or more of AI projects runs 26, 53, 64 and 89 percent across the four tiers. The average share of agentic projects with outcomes runs 34, 45, 54 and 67 percent, moving in step with the share of organisations running several agents in production. Reading the tiers as road-map stages, deployment and success rise together. Because the maturity score itself includes outcomes as an input, part of this relationship is definitional. Theme: Outlook. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Deliver measurable outcomes on half or more of AI projects, by tier; Average share of agentic AI projects delivering outcomes, by tier; Organisations with several AI agents already in production, by maturity tier. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 3, 7, 8, 17, 18.

chunks.title: Neither company size nor industry buys maturity
chunks.text: Real-time data maturity and AI success are flat from 500-employee firms to those with 10,000 or more, and industry gaps are modest compared with the gaps between maturity tiers. IDC's maturity scores sit between 50 and 53 across all company-size bands and AI success between 46 and 51 percent. By industry, healthcare, education and software lead modestly on both measures. Retail has the lowest maturity score at 48 and ties with manufacturing and financial services for the lowest AI success rate, at 47 percent. Even so, the industry spread is far smaller than the tier spread. IDC's conclusion is that maturity is earned through operating practices, not headcount. On the supply side, AIM finds that vendors of every size, specialism and stage of maturity describe much the same delivery problems, which points to difficulties shared across the market. Theme: Adoption and production. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Real-time data maturity score by industry; Share of AI projects with measurable outcomes, by industry; Real-time data maturity score by company size (employees). Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 9, 10; AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 11.

chunks.title: As organisations mature, real-time data talent moves into the business
chunks.text: Leaders are more likely to embed real-time data talent in the business teams that use it, and service providers' delivery teams include forward-deployed engineers and domain expert benches that also bring technical skill close to the business. IDC finds talent embedded in business teams rising from 21 percent of Emerging organisations to 34 percent of Leaders, while distributed and loosely coordinated talent falls from 60 to 37 percent. On the supply side, AIM describes forward-deployed or embedded AI engineers who work inside client environments to bridge business and technical teams and improve conversion, and two models for domain expertise: SMEs drawn from a shared pool as needed, or a large standing bench of specialists who validate outputs and run quality checks. Even among Leaders, embedded talent is still only about one in three. Theme: Talent and organisation. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Real-time data talent embedded in business teams, by tier; Real-time data talent distributed and not embedded, by tier; Recurring role types in a GenAI delivery team. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 16; AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 23, 24.

chunks.title: Optimism and hype fatigue coexist
chunks.text: Four in five enterprise leaders say agentic AI is changing how they work, and seven in ten say it is overhyped. Vendors list unrealistic expectations as a recurring delivery problem. IDC's respondents agree at 80 percent that agentic AI is changing the way they work and at 79 percent that it is making the world better, while 71 percent agree it is overhyped. The two views are held simultaneously. AIM's vendor study includes hype-inflated expectations from stakeholders in a wider set of challenges that several vendors mention, without ranking them by frequency. The practical implication is that expectation-setting and value-case discipline are part of delivery, not just sales. Public opinion mirrors it: global optimism rose to 59% in 2025, while nervousness also rose, to 52%. BCG's executive respondents name the top three AI risks less often than a year earlier, even as they expect AI spending to roughly double as a share of revenue in 2026. Theme: Market state. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Sentiment about agentic AI; Global public sentiment about AI, 2022 to 2025 (Ipsos AI Monitor); Top AI concerns among executives. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 20; AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 10; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 363; Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 6, 8.

chunks.title: Real-time data investments are meeting expectations almost everywhere
chunks.text: About nine in ten organisations say their real-time data investments met or exceeded expectations, rising to 97 or 98 percent among Leaders. IDC reports business outcomes met or exceeded at 85, 93, 97 and 97 percent across the four tiers and performance metrics at 87, 94, 97 and 98 percent. Satisfaction is high in every tier and increases with maturity. Given the sponsor's interest in this finding and the self-reported nature of the measure, it is best read as a sentiment indicator. Theme: Outlook. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Real-time data investments met or exceeded expected business outcomes, by tier. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 19.

chunks.title: The near-term agenda: data quality first, then GenAI and agentic support
chunks.text: For real-time data over the next 12 to 18 months, improving data and analytics quality is the top strategic objective, with support for GenAI and agentic use cases tied for second alongside analytics efficiency. IDC's respondents rank improving data and analytics quality first at 33 percent. Supporting GenAI and agentic AI use cases and improving analytics efficiency tie at 27 percent, with process automation, app-to-app integration and reducing time from data to decision at 26 percent each. The ordering matches the challenge data, where data quality and consistency is the top technical barrier for real-time data at 46 percent: fix the data, then build on it. Theme: Outlook. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Top strategic objectives for real-time data, next 12 to 18 months. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 13, 21.

chunks.title: What GenAI engagements cost, by stage
chunks.text: Pilots typically run 40 to 80 thousand dollars, single-business-unit production 150 to 300 thousand, and enterprise-wide programmes 500 thousand to more than a million, with the largest reaching 2 to 4 million or more. AIM's pricing benchmarks give a range and a typical cluster for each stage. Proofs of concept and pilots range from about 25 to 100 thousand dollars, with some leaders above 150 thousand. Production for a single business unit ranges 100 to 500 thousand depending on integrations and scope. Scaled, enterprise-wide programmes range from 300 thousand to more than 2 million, typically 500 thousand to a million or more. AIM presents these as project price ranges and does not say whether platform licences or model usage are included. Theme: Pricing and engagement. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: GenAI engagement price by stage (USD, thousands). Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 21.

chunks.title: Managed services are the fastest-growing engagement model; outcome-linked pricing is rising but rare
chunks.text: Project-based work remains the entry point, run-and-operate contracts are growing fastest as production deployments increase, and only a few vendors tie part of their fees to outcomes. AIM maps six engagement models. Fixed-scope or time-and-materials projects dominate pilots and early production. Capacity-led pods are widely used as programmes expand. Run-and-operate managed services are growing fastest. Outcome-linked pricing is selective but rising in mature, KPI-driven deployments, and platform subscriptions are emerging among IP-led vendors. In the vendor profiles, only a handful describe outcome- or value-linked constructs, and one, Neoware, works only on fixed-scope or outcome-based terms. Vendors mature enough to align fees with results are positioned for a market moving toward accountability. Theme: Pricing and engagement. Evidence: single-source. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 22, 44, 60, 70.

chunks.title: GenAI delivery teams cluster around six to eight roles, with agentic specialists emerging
chunks.text: Data scientists and LLM engineers are the largest group, supported by data engineers, LLMOps engineers, architects, domain translators, embedded engineers, application developers and delivery governance. A distinct agentic AI architect role is appearing. AIM finds team structures converge on six to eight recurring role types despite differing names. Data scientists, ML engineers and LLM engineers consistently form the largest share, sometimes split between model-performance scientists and application-layer LLM engineers. Data engineers own pipelines, vector stores and RAG foundations. LLMOps engineers own CI/CD, serving, monitoring and cost. Domain consultants and business translators handle value mapping and adoption. Some vendors now count agentic AI architects as a separate headcount category for orchestration and tool-calling frameworks; most still fold this into the general pool. Theme: Talent and organisation. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Recurring role types in a GenAI delivery team. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 23, 24.

chunks.title: Domain specialisation concentrates in BFSI, healthcare and life sciences, retail and supply chain
chunks.text: Most vendors run a hybrid strategy of reusable horizontal capabilities plus a few deep verticals, and the deepest verticals are regulated or data-rich industries. AIM finds hybrid strategies are the norm and that deep specialisation is most evident in banking and financial services, healthcare, retail and supply chain, the sectors where GenAI now sits inside core operations. Our count of the 28 vendor profiles supports this: financial services appears in more than 20 industry lists and healthcare or life sciences in more than 15. AIM's industry use-case matrix gives financial services, with eight entries, and healthcare and life sciences the longest lists of agentic use cases, such as underwriting, claims audit, regulatory dossier automation and medical, legal and regulatory review in pharma. Theme: Vendor landscape. Evidence: agent-analysis. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 16, 17.

chunks.title: Pairing large domain expert benches with agents is a Leader strategy
chunks.text: Three of the ten Leaders build domain-expert teams into their AI delivery. Two report benches of at least 6,000 specialists, and one pairs analysts and agents under maker-checker controls with full source traceability to reassure regulated buyers. Two vendors report benches of at least 6,000 domain specialists. At one, analysts and agents carry out tasks together on a shared platform, and at the other, specialists review what the models produce and keep quality under watch while work is under way. A third describes its delivery as pairing domain SMEs with AI tooling in selected workflows such as financial spreading and credit decisioning. All three sit in the Leaders quadrant. This is the standing-bench model AIM describes, more common at vendors with managed-services or knowledge-process-outsourcing roots, and AIM notes in one of these profiles that it gives a compliance story that technology-only providers could match only by hiring comparable teams. Platform access is sometimes priced as an uplift on existing analyst fees. Theme: Vendor landscape. Evidence: agent-analysis. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 24, 33, 34, 49, 75, 76.

chunks.title: Hyperscaler and lakehouse partnerships are common; partner tier is the differentiator
chunks.text: Most vendors list the same few platforms: Databricks in 25 of 28 profiles, AWS and Microsoft Azure in 23 each, Google Cloud in 18 and Snowflake in 17. Vendors distinguish themselves by premier or select partner status and early access to new platform capabilities. Across the 28 profiles the same handful of platforms recurs, and 12 vendors list all five of Databricks, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Snowflake, so listing them conveys little. The differentiators cited are tier and depth: top-percentile partner status, generative AI competencies, select cohorts limited to a few dozen partners globally, gold-level data-platform status with certified staff, and pre-launch access to agentic and model services that lets a vendor experiment ahead of the market. Some vendors also run joint go-to-market and co-sell programmes with these platforms. Theme: Vendor landscape. Evidence: agent-analysis. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 44, 50, 66, 70.

chunks.title: Synthetic personas and audiences are an emerging product category
chunks.text: At least two Leaders sell simulation platforms that test products, messaging or pricing against AI-generated customer segments before real-market research. One vendor reports a persona simulation platform with a stated correlation of 95 percent or more with real behaviour, used for product testing, pricing and UX validation. Another reports synthetic customer cohorts for concept and message testing deployed in production for consumer goods and technology clients, with one launch cycle cut from nine months to two or three. AIM's service taxonomy lists synthetic audiences and virtual personas under application development, indicating the category has become a recognised offering. Theme: Market state. Evidence: agent-analysis. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13, 43, 45, 46.

chunks.title: Disclosed conversion rates are selectively reported
chunks.text: The few vendors that publish a pilot-to-production figure report rates above 60 percent, well above the 25 to 45 percent AIM says is typical. Read undisclosed as probably typical. Three vendors state a conversion rate: more than 60 percent, 70 percent, and 80 percent or more. At least five others describe their rate as high or above industry average without a number. Since AIM characterises most vendors as converting 25 to 45 percent, the disclosed figures are best read as the top of the distribution rather than representative. All are vendor-claimed and unaudited by the publisher. Buyers can treat a vendor's willingness to state and evidence a number as a signal in itself. Theme: Method and caveats. Evidence: agent-analysis. Related statistics: Typical POC-to-production conversion rate across vendors; Vendor-disclosed POC-to-production conversion rates. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 32, 36, 44, 52, 60, 64, 76, 84, 89.

chunks.title: The 2026 PeMa Quadrant: ten Leaders, and reach and maturity do not always go together
chunks.text: Ten of 28 vendors are Leaders. The highest-reach vendor and the highest-maturity vendor are different firms, and several highly mature vendors sit outside the Leaders quadrant on reach alone. AIM places 10 vendors in Leaders, 9 in Seasoned Vendors, 3 in Growth Vendors and 6 in Challengers. Tiger Analytics leads on Penetration at 0.90 and Blend360 on Maturity at 0.95. The Seasoned Vendors quadrant contains firms whose maturity scores rival the Leaders but whose market reach lags, for example a vendor ranked seventh on maturity but fifteenth on penetration. Growth Vendors show the reverse pattern. Because participation is voluntary, the quadrant covers the 28 firms that took part, not the whole market. Theme: Vendor landscape. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Vendors per PeMa quadrant, 2026; Penetration (Pe) index by vendor; Maturity (Ma) index by vendor. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 26, 28, 29.

chunks.title: Five things real-time data leaders do differently
chunks.text: Treat real-time data as core AI infrastructure, consolidate onto one platform, use governance as an accelerator, connect agents to live enterprise context, and invest ahead of the curve. IDC closes with five priorities that separate leading organisations. First, treat real-time, event-driven data as core AI infrastructure rather than an analytics afterthought. Second, consolidate fragmented tooling onto a unified, integrated platform, the clearest marker of a leader. Third, reframe governance as an accelerator rather than a brake. Fourth, connect agents to real-time enterprise context, since lack of context is the top barrier to production. Fifth, invest ahead of the curve: IDC states that 94 to 97 percent plan to increase real-time data and agentic investment, and the two rise together. Theme: Outlook. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Plan to increase real-time data and agentic AI investment; Run a single unified real-time data platform, by tier; Top barriers to scaling AI agents. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 22.

chunks.title: How to test a GenAI service provider: look for a production track record, not a capability list
chunks.text: Probe which accelerators run in production for clients, ask for named deployments with quantified outcomes, and ask how agent behaviour is evaluated and governed. Drawing on AIM's analyst guidance across the report, three tests recur. On accelerators, ask which have been deployed in production client engagements versus internal tools repackaged as client-ready. On agentic claims, the credible vendors can explain how their agents are actually built, point to live production deployments and say how agent behaviour is tested and controlled; others label any multi-step flow as agentic. On challenges, the gap is widening between vendors that have engineered solutions to the known problems and those that merely name them, and buyers are learning to test for it earlier in procurement. AIM also reminds readers its report is one input and not a recommendation. Theme: Vendor landscape. Evidence: single-source. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 6, 11, 15, 89.

chunks.title: Outlook: spending keeps rising, and the constraint is operational
chunks.text: The vendors that last will be those with proven production deployments, real platforms, industry specialisation and the operating machinery to run AI at scale. Investment is set to keep rising on both the real-time data and agentic fronts. AIM expects the market's next phase to reward proof over promise: not the fullest description of the lifecycle, but repeated evidence of having run it at scale. IDC finds near-universal intent to increase spending on real-time data and agentic AI, with the two rising together, while the near-term agenda puts data quality first. Taken together, the sources point to a market where the constraint is operational: data foundations, governance, adoption and cost discipline determine who converts intent into outcomes. Theme: Outlook. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Plan to increase real-time data and agentic AI investment; Top strategic objectives for real-time data, next 12 to 18 months. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 7; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 21, 22.

chunks.title: How to read these two sources
chunks.text: One is a voluntary vendor study with unaudited self-reported data; the other is a vendor-sponsored buyer survey whose maturity score includes the outcomes it then correlates with. Both are useful, with those caveats. The AIM study covers 28 vendors that chose to participate, scored from questionnaires, briefings and secondary research; vendor-submitted data is not independently audited and the publisher states it is not a recommendation. The IDC survey of 623 large-enterprise decision-makers is sponsored by a real-time data platform vendor, its framing matches the sponsor's interest, and its composite maturity score includes real-time deployment and outcomes as inputs, so correlations between maturity and those measures are partly built in. Our meta-analysis restates both in our own words, cites every figure, and gives more weight to findings where the two independent methods agree. Theme: Method and caveats. Evidence: agent-analysis. Related statistics: GenAI service providers evaluated in the AIM 2026 study; IDC survey sample. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 26, 89; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 3, 8, 27, 28.

chunks.title: Six practice areas for running GenAI at scale
chunks.text: Vendors converge on six areas of practice: holding down cost and compute, using tokens efficiently, watching live systems, governing risk, securing data and meeting compliance, and tracking the value delivered. AIM sorts the practices vendors describe for large deployments into six areas. On cost, vendors match model size to the task, route work across several models, design around retrieval first, and compress, cache and batch requests. On performance, they trim context, combine retrieval methods, give prompts a fixed structure and run agent steps in parallel. On monitoring, they track tokens, spend, latency and accuracy as they happen, watch for drift and hallucination, roll out changes in stages and trace pipelines end to end. On governance, they apply responsible-AI controls, keep people involved in high-stakes decisions, keep version control and maintain audit trails. On security, they restrict access, mask personal data, deploy privately and align with compliance standards. On value, they measure against KPIs, reuse assets and keep refining over time. Theme: Operations and LLMOps. Evidence: single-source. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20.

chunks.title: Security and trust are the second-biggest driver of real-time data demand
chunks.text: Security and AI trust requirements rank second among drivers of real-time data need and governance is a top-five technical challenge, which is why IDC tells buyers to treat governance as an accelerator. In the IDC survey, 40 percent cite security and AI trust requirements as a driver of increased need for real-time data, just behind agentic AI at 43. Governance, security and permissions is a top technical challenge at 39 percent. IDC's advice is to reframe governance from a brake to an accelerator, noting it is already a leading investment priority. AIM's synthesis of vendor responses agrees from the delivery side, listing guardrails, audit trails, role-based access and compliance with recognised standards among the practices vendors use to run GenAI at scale. BCG's survey of executives and Deloitte's enterprise survey both rank privacy and security as the top AI concern, with 53% of BCG respondents naming it. In BCG's data, 32% of executives see cybersecurity as the biggest opportunity from agentic AI and 9% as the biggest threat, while 59% see it as both. Theme: Governance and trust. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Most significant drivers of increased need for real-time data; Top technical challenges for real-time data, next 12 to 18 months; Top AI concerns among executives; How leaders see AI agents in cybersecurity; AI risks organisations are most concerned about. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 6, 13, 22; AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20; Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 2, 8, 9; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 21.

chunks.title: Enterprise spend on generative AI reached about $37 billion in 2025, more than tripling
chunks.text: Menlo Ventures sizes 2025 enterprise generative AI spend at about $37B, up 3.2x, split almost evenly between infrastructure and applications. Per-company budgets and capital-market data point the same way. Menlo's bottom-up model excludes chips, inference hosting and AI features bundled into existing software, so it understates total AI outlay. Within its scope, model APIs took $12.5B and applications $19B, where horizontal AI ($8.4B, mostly copilots at $7.2B) was the biggest segment and coding ($4.0B) the biggest single use case. a16z's Global 2000 CIOs report average LLM spend of about $7M per firm in 2025, up from $2.5M actually spent in 2024 (the prose cites a $4.5M baseline that was a forecast), and average application spend of about $5.8M per firm against a planned $3.9M. Stanford's compilation of Quid data shows private AI investment of about $345B in the same year, an order of magnitude larger because it measures capital into AI companies rather than enterprise purchases. All three lenses more than doubled in 2025. Theme: Market state. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Enterprise generative AI spend by year (USD billions); Generative AI spend by category, 2023 to 2025 (USD billions); Average enterprise spend on LLMs (USD millions); Average enterprise spend on AI applications (USD millions); Global private AI investment (USD billions, Quid). Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 178, 179.

chunks.title: AI budgets are still rising in 2026, but expectations for the pace moderated during the year
chunks.text: Early-2026 surveys expected AI spend to rise steeply, roughly doubling in BCG's data and growing about 65% in a16z's; mid-2026 surveys show continued growth at a lower rate. Growth is not in doubt, the rate is. In BCG's AI Radar, published in January 2026, the 2,360 executives surveyed, 640 of them CEOs, expected AI investment to rise from 0.8% to 1.7% of revenue during the year, and a16z's CIOs projected 65% growth in LLM spend. In surveys fielded between late April and June, McKinsey found 60% of respondents at organisations using AI expecting to increase AI investment but only 8% by 30% or more, and KPMG's large US firms put projected 12-month AI spend at $202M, close to the $207M of the quarter before and more than double the $88M of a year earlier. Every source still shows growth, and BCG found 94% would keep investing even if 2026 returns disappointed. The time ordering matters: the two surveys fielded latest show the softest profile. Our reading is a market moving from step change to steady growth, which the 2027 editions will confirm or refute. Theme: Market state. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Average AI investment as a share of company revenue; What executives would do if AI failed to pay off within 12 months; Average enterprise spend on LLMs (USD millions); Expected change in AI investment next year; Average projected AI investment over the next 12 months, by quarter (USD millions). Sources: Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 2, 5, 6; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 16; KPMG US, 2026, pages 3.

chunks.title: Coding is generative AI's first killer use case
chunks.text: Software development is where spend, measured productivity, vendor competition and scaled agent use all concentrate. Coding tools were about $4B in 2025, five times the prior year. Menlo puts coding at more than half of departmental AI spend, with code agents growing from near zero to $1.1B and half of developers using AI coding tools daily. Stanford's table of micro-level productivity studies, whose methods vary, includes one study in which developers using GitHub Copilot completed 26% more pull requests, with junior and less experienced developers gaining most. McKinsey finds about a fifth of organisations scaling coding agents in mid-2026, rising to 31% at large firms, and a third have declined to buy software because coding agents let them build it. a16z finds Anthropic leading in software development, where CIOs credit rapid capability gains for adoption, and its own analysis attributes much of Anthropic's gain in wallet share to token-heavy coding work. Lightcast data in the AI Index show US AI job postings naming the Agentic AI skill rising from 151 in 2024 to 16,541 in 2025, more than a hundredfold. The pattern is consistent: verifiable, structured work with a paying developer audience adopts first. Theme: Market state. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Departmental AI spend by department, 2025 (USD millions); AI coding spend by segment, 2024 vs 2025 (USD millions); Developers using AI coding tools daily; AI tools at the scaling phase, small vs large organisations; Declined at least one software purchase because coding agents could build it in-house, by industry; US job postings mentioning agentic AI skills, 2024 vs 2025 (Lightcast); Measured productivity effects of AI in micro-level studies. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 208, 219, 220; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 3, 7, 9; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: Startups are winning AI applications while incumbents hold infrastructure and the enterprise seat
chunks.text: AI-native startups took about 63% of application revenue in 2025, yet 94% of the 100 Global 2000 firms in a16z's survey pay for Microsoft 365 Copilot and 65% prefer an incumbent when one exists. Menlo's revenue data show startups ahead in departmental (60%), vertical (88%) and horizontal (57%) applications but behind in infrastructure (44%), where application builders stay on established data platforms. a16z's Global 2000 survey shows the other side: 94% pay for Microsoft 365 Copilot, 74% for GitHub Copilot, and 65% prefer incumbents, citing trust, integration and easier procurement. Startups are chosen for faster innovation and deeper AI focus. MIT NANDA's interviews add that a trusted vendor is the top selection criterion and that many procurement leaders wait for an incumbent's AI feature rather than evaluate startups. The two pictures fit a market where incumbents own the broad seat licence and startups own the high-value, high-token workloads. Theme: Vendor landscape. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Startup share of AI application revenue; Startup vs incumbent revenue share by layer, 2025; Startup share of departmental AI revenue, by department; Adoption of incumbent AI applications among Global 2000 respondents; Enterprises that prefer incumbent solutions when available; Why enterprises prefer existing software vendors; Why enterprises prefer AI-native startups; Vendor selection criteria mentioned by buyers (approximate). Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 15, 16.

chunks.title: Who leads enterprise LLMs depends on who is counting, but the direction of travel is shared
chunks.text: Menlo ranks Anthropic first by API usage; a16z ranks OpenAI first by production footprint among Global 2000 firms. Each firm invests in the vendor it places first. Both agree Anthropic is gaining fastest and Google is rising, while falling open-weight share is Menlo's finding alone and widespread multi-model use is a16z's. Menlo estimates Anthropic at 40% of enterprise LLM API usage in 2025, OpenAI 27% and Google 21%, from a US sample of 495 that includes AI-native builders and weights by application scale. a16z finds 78% of Global 2000 respondents using OpenAI in production and a 56% average wallet share, with Anthropic at 44% production use and 17% wallet share, from 100 large firms with coding startups excluded. Read together, OpenAI has the widest footprint in large incumbents' estates and Anthropic has the larger share of token-intensive coding work and the fastest growth. Menlo puts open-source models at 11% of enterprise usage, down from 19%, while a16z reports a growing preference for closed models. a16z finds 81% of large enterprises using three or more model families and a move away from fine-tuning toward prompting and routing, while Menlo's single snapshot finds prompt design dominant and fine-tuning rare. The site presents both estimates with their samples and conflicts of interest and does not declare a single leader. Theme: Vendor landscape. Evidence: agent-analysis. Related statistics: Enterprise LLM API share by vendor, 2023 to 2025 (Menlo estimate); Coding model share, 2025 (Menlo estimate); Open-weight models' share of enterprise LLM usage; Enterprises using each model vendor in production, by survey wave; Average share of LLM spend by vendor, 2024 to 2026 expected (a16z); Enterprises using three or more model families in testing or production; Customers running each vendor's most capable models; Preference for open vs closed models, Jan 2026. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: Buying beats building, in five sources, with one new counter-current from coding agents
chunks.text: Purchased AI use cases rose from 53% to 76% in a year, bought solutions reach production about twice as often as internal builds, and third-party applications are gaining share, with many enterprises expecting to move from in-house model builds to packaged applications over time. McKinsey adds that a third have declined a software purchase because coding agents let them build it. Menlo's survey shows the purchase share jumping to 76% and bought AI converting to production at 47% against 25% for conventional software. MIT NANDA's interviews find externally sourced tools reaching deployment about 66% of the time versus 33% for internal builds, with roughly double the employee usage. a16z's chart shows the third-party application share rising in all five use cases it tracks, and AIM's own market analysis finds buyers now judging providers on what they have run in production rather than on what they say they can build. Deloitte's pilot-trap diagnosis explains why: production needs infrastructure, integration, security review, compliance checks and monitoring that a small, isolated pilot can do without. McKinsey's mid-2026 finding that 32% have forgone a purchase in favour of building with coding agents, rising to about half of high performers, is not a contradiction: enterprises buy applications and platforms and build the long tail of features they once bought. It is early survey evidence that agentic coding is changing software budgets. Theme: Pricing and engagement. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: AI use cases purchased vs built in-house; Pilot-to-production funnel, AI purchases vs traditional software; Deployment success rate by sourcing approach; Share choosing a third-party application over building on a raw model, May 2025 vs Jan 2026; Declined at least one software purchase because coding agents could build it in-house, by industry; Declined a software purchase in favour of building with coding agents, high performers vs others. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 19, 20; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026; AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6, 8; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 9; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 9, 21.

chunks.title: Healthcare buys packaged vertical AI; regulated finance buys services instead
chunks.text: Healthcare took about 43% of vertical AI software spend in 2025, led by ambient scribes, while finance and insurance software markets stayed tiny even though financial services is one of the deepest specialisations among AI service providers. Menlo's vertical spend data put healthcare at $1.5B, more than the next three verticals combined (legal, creator tools and government, $1.36B; Menlo's text says the next four, but its chart puts those four at $1.54B), with finance at $120M and insurance under $100M. By our count, 24 of AIM's 28 vendor profiles list a financial-services industry, and AIM sees provider specialisation running deepest in healthcare, BFSI, retail and supply chain. The reconciliation is that regulated financial institutions buy custom, services-led delivery with compliance blueprints rather than packaged products, which is exactly the market AIM's providers serve, while healthcare found a packaged product (clinical documentation) with immediate, measurable relief from administrative burden. NANDA's disruption index does not separate the two sectors, since it scores healthcare and financial services equally at 0.5, but its notes fit the picture: healthcare activity is documentation pilots with clinical models unchanged, while finance activity is backend automation with customer relationships stable. Theme: Vendor landscape. Evidence: agent-analysis. Related statistics: Vertical AI spend by industry, 2025 (USD millions); AI Market Disruption Index by sector (0 to 5). Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 5.

chunks.title: Where AI is built now matters as much as what it does: sovereignty has become a planning input
chunks.text: More than four in five surveyed AI-adopting companies treat data residency and local compute as at least moderately important, three quarters weigh a vendor's country of origin, and publics trust the EU more than the US or China to regulate AI. Deloitte's survey of leaders at organisations with working AI, fielded August to September 2025, found 83% rating data-residency and in-country compute at least moderately important to strategic planning, 66% at least moderately concerned about reliance on foreign-owned AI, 77% factoring country of origin into vendor selection and 58% building their stacks mainly with local vendors. The pressure is regional: 11% of Americas firms source most of their stack abroad against 32% in EMEA. Stanford's compilation adds the demand-side signal that, in Pew's 25-country survey, a median of 53% trusts the EU to regulate AI versus 37% for the US and 27% for China, and that in a separate Ipsos survey of 30 countries US respondents show the least trust in their own government to regulate AI, at 31%. a16z's sample of 100 Global 2000 firms operating across North America, the UK, the EU, Asia and Australia, with no regional split published, shows the opposite motion, with four in five hosting models directly with frontier labs, so differences in sample make-up may explain part of the gap. No other source in this project measures sovereignty directly, so the Deloitte figures stand alone on the enterprise side. Theme: Governance and trust. Evidence: single-source. Related statistics: Importance of data residency and local compute in strategic planning; Concern about reliance on foreign-owned AI technology and compute; Organisations that weigh an AI solution's country of origin in vendor selection; Organisations building their AI stack mainly with local vendors; Organisations sourcing the majority of their AI stack from foreign vendors, by region; Trust own government to regulate AI, by country, 2025 (Ipsos); Trust to regulate AI effectively, 25-country median (Pew 2025); Enterprises hosting models directly with a frontier lab. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 5, 15, 16, 33, 40; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 380, 381; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: Physical AI is in most adopters’ operations, led by Asia Pacific, but robot installations were flat in 2024
chunks.text: Deloitte finds 58% of AI-using companies already use robotics, drones or automated machinery to some extent, and respondents expect 80% to do so within two years. Robot installation data temper the pace: global installations were flat in 2024 and US installations fell. In Deloitte's survey, Asia Pacific leads with 71% reporting at least minimal physical AI use against 56% in the Americas and EMEA, and expected use reaches 90% in Asia Pacific. Intelligent monitoring, collaborative robots and digital twins are the types expected to matter most, and cost is the barrier cited most often, while Deloitte separately notes that facility retrofits, hardware, integration and maintenance can far exceed the spend on AI models and software. The International Federation of Robotics data compiled by Stanford show 542,000 industrial robots installed in 2024, up 0.2%, with China at 54% of the world and the US down 9%; collaborative robots reached 13.6% of installations. Microsoft's agent telemetry shows manufacturing and resources at about a tenth of agent-using firms but about 17% of agents, a sign of deployment at scale within each firm. Physical AI is real and concentrated in Asia and in controlled environments; the two-year jump to 80% is an expectation, not a trend. Theme: Adoption and production. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Organisations using physical AI at least to a limited extent; Physical AI use by region, today vs in two years; Types of physical AI expected to have the greatest impact; Industrial robot installations and stock, 2024 (IFR); Industrial robot installations by country, 2024 (thousands, IFR); Agent adoption by industry: share of firms using agents vs share of all agents (telemetry, approximate). Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 6, 22, 23, 24, 25, 27; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 227, 228, 229, 230; Microsoft, 2026, pages 18.

chunks.title: Agent adoption figures range from single digits to more than half, and the definition explains the spread
chunks.text: Sources report agent use anywhere from low single digits to 59% because they measure different things: any use, self-reported moderate use, deployment, scaling, or an architectural test of what counts as an agent. On the most inclusive measure, McKinsey puts organisational AI use at 88% for 2025, as compiled by Stanford, and at 89% in its own 2026 survey. Self-reported agent use follows: KPMG finds 53% of large US firms with agents deployed, IDC 20% to 59% by maturity tier with several agents in production, Deloitte 23% using agentic AI at least moderately. Stage-based measures fall further: McKinsey finds 22% of firms under $1B and 40% of $1B-plus firms scaling agents in at least one function, while its 2025 data put scaled agent use in single digits for nearly all functions. The strictest measures are architectural: Menlo classifies 16% of enterprise deployments as true agents that plan, act, observe and adapt, and a16z finds agentic workflow automation in production at 13%. The ladder from any use to scaled, governed agents is the finding. The site places each source on it rather than quoting one number. Theme: Agentic AI. Evidence: agent-analysis. Related statistics: Organisations using AI in at least one function (McKinsey 2025 via the Index); AI agents at scaling or fully scaled stage, by function (McKinsey 2025 via the Index); AI agent deployment rate among large US firms; Organisations with several AI agents already in production, by maturity tier; Organisations using agentic AI at least moderately; Extent of AI agent use by company size, 2025 vs 2026; Deployments that qualify as true agentic systems; AI use cases in production among Global 2000 respondents. Sources: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 193, 198; KPMG US, 2026, pages 6; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 8; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 17; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 3, 5, 6; Menlo Ventures, 2025; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: One in four has 40% or more of experiments in production; what you buy converts better than what you build
