Our expectation is steady expansion of intelligent monitoring, cobots and digital twins in controlled settings, led by Asia Pacific, and slower progress in open environments where safety regulation and liability apply. Theme: Outlook. Evidence: multi-source. Related statistics: Organisations using physical AI at least to a limited extent; Physical AI use by region, today vs in two years; Types of physical AI expected to have the greatest impact; Industrial robot installations and stock, 2024 (IFR); Industrial robot installations by country, 2024 (thousands, IFR); Agent adoption by industry: share of firms using agents vs share of all agents (telemetry, approximate); Vertical AI spend by industry, 2025 (USD millions). Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 22, 23, 24, 25, 27; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 227, 228, 229, 230; Microsoft, 2026, pages 18; Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Outlook: where the sources disagree, and why
chunks.text: Five disagreements run through the twelve sources: which model vendor leads, whether company size matters, how many pilots fail, how fast spend grows, and how many jobs go. In each case the sources measure different things or different populations, and the notes record the reconciliation. Vendor leadership: Menlo (Anthropic, API usage, broad US sample, Anthropic investor) versus a16z (OpenAI, production footprint and wallet share among Global 2000 firms, OpenAI investor); both agree on direction. Size: McKinsey and the AI Index show large firms far ahead on deployment stage; IDC and AIM show maturity and delivery challenges flat by size; breadth of deployment is not maturity of practice. Failure: NANDA's 5% success is custom tools that showed a marked, sustained productivity or P&L effect when measured six months after the pilot; AIM's 25% to 45% is vendor POCs; Menlo's 47% is bought solutions; Deloitte's 25% is firms past a production threshold. Spend: January surveys expected steep growth, with BCG seeing investment as a share of revenue roughly double and a16z seeing average LLM spend rise about 65%, while KPMG's late April to May pulse shows planned investment holding steady. Jobs: 39% of McKinsey respondents expect headcount to fall and Deloitte firms expect at least a tenth of jobs to be fully automated (36% within a year, 82% within three years), which measures automation rather than headcount, against 14% of McKinsey respondents reporting actual cuts and NANDA's limited layoffs. The site presents each pair with its definitions rather than picking a side, because the disagreement itself is the finding readers need. Theme: Outlook. Evidence: agent-analysis. Related statistics: Enterprise LLM API share by vendor, 2023 to 2025 (Menlo estimate); Average share of LLM spend by vendor, 2024 to 2026 expected (a16z); Scaling AI enterprise-wide, by company size; Real-time data maturity score by company size (employees); Adoption funnel, embedded or task-specific GenAI tools; Typical POC-to-production conversion rate across vendors; Pilot-to-production funnel, AI purchases vs traditional software; Organisations that have moved 40% or more of AI experiments into production; Expected vs reported change in total headcount because of AI. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 6, 25; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 197; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 10; AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 11; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 6, 7, 24; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 8, 12; Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 6; KPMG US, 2026, pages 3.

chunks.title: Outlook: eight indicators to watch in the 2027 editions
chunks.text: The next round of these reports will show whether the 2026 expectations held. The notes name the specific numbers to compare. One: Deloitte's share of firms with 40% or more of experiments in production, expected to rise from 25% to 54%. Two: McKinsey's EBIT attribution (37%) and high-performer share (6%), both unchanged between the 2025 and 2026 surveys. Three: a16z's ROI distribution, currently half at break-even or worse, and its wallet-share trend for Anthropic, Google and OpenAI. Four: KPMG's agent deployment rate (53%) and orchestration share (18%), the earliest read on whether the plateau persists. Five: McKinsey's reported versus expected headcount change, currently 14% against 39%. Six: the share of organisations with mature agent governance (Deloitte 21%) and mitigating unauthorised agent action (McKinsey 33% outside the high-performer group, 45% among high performers). Seven: BCG's investment as a share of revenue, expected to reach 1.7%. Eight: Menlo's agent-platform spend against copilots, currently $750M against $7.2B, and Quid's agent investment against it. Movement on these eight will tell readers whether 2026 was the year agents moved from pilots to production or the year expectations were reset. Theme: Outlook. Evidence: agent-analysis. Related statistics: Organisations that have moved 40% or more of AI experiments into production; Organisations attributing a positive EBIT impact to AI; AI high performers (5%+ of EBIT from AI and significant value); Estimated ROI on LLM spend, Jan 2026; Average share of LLM spend by vendor, 2024 to 2026 expected (a16z); AI agent deployment rate among large US firms; Stage of AI agent adoption, Q1 vs Q2 2026; Expected vs reported change in total headcount because of AI; Organisations with a mature governance model for autonomous agents; AI risks organisations are actively mitigating, high performers vs others; Average AI investment as a share of company revenue; Horizontal AI spend by category, 2025 (USD millions); Private AI investment by focus area, 2025 (USD billions, Quid). Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 8, 20; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 3, 12, 17, 23, 25; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026; KPMG US, 2026, pages 6; Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 6; Menlo Ventures, 2025; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 187.

chunks.title: Aays
chunks.text: Aays, founded 2018, headquartered in Singapore, Singapore. AIM Research 2026 PeMa Quadrant: Seasoned Vendors. Penetration score 0.47 (rank 14 of 28), Maturity score 0.67 (rank 10 of 28). Focus: Decision intelligence embedded in supply chain, finance and operations workflows, delivered through prebuilt agent frameworks and command-centre style control towers. Industries: FMCG and consumer goods, Automotive and manufacturing, Retail and e-commerce, BFSI and fintech. Markets: United States, Europe, Asia Pacific and Japan. Named platforms and accelerators: AaDi (Agentic decision intelligence over structured data); AutoDBX (ETL and data migration accelerator); CFO Intelligence (Finance copilot); Agent Factory (Multi-agent orchestration); GenAI Risk Monitor + Digital Twin (Simulates risk scenarios against a digital twin); Control Towers (Domain command centres). Differentiators: GenAI wired into planning and execution rather than an assistive layer; Marketplace of reusable agents and data modules; Rapid maturity gain from 2024 to 2026 with a shift to production-led work; Digital twin and simulation for scenario evaluation; Multi-business-unit and multi-geography expansions. Vendor-claimed metrics (unaudited): POC-to-production conversion: High (no figure); Repeat-client share: Strong (no figure). Partners: Microsoft Azure, Databricks, Google Cloud, Dremio. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 31, 32.

chunks.title: Acuity Analytics
chunks.text: Acuity Analytics, founded 2002, headquartered in London, United Kingdom. AIM Research 2026 PeMa Quadrant: Leaders. Penetration score 0.55 (rank 10 of 28), Maturity score 0.65 (rank 11 of 28). Focus: Financial services specialist pairing a very large analyst workforce with AI agents in a human-in-the-loop operating model for banking, asset management, private markets and insurance. Industries: Banking, Asset management, Private markets, Insurance, Professional services and legal, Industrials. Markets: United States, United Kingdom, Europe, UAE, India. Named platforms and accelerators: Agent Fleet (Model-agnostic agentic platform with 50+ prebuilt financial workflows); RFP Pulse (Bid and RFP response automation); IntelliGRID (Due diligence with premium financial data sources); Guidelines Compliance Manager (Investment compliance automation); Financial Modeling Excel-native agents (Chat-driven spreadsheet generation). Differentiators: Two decades of front and middle-office financial services delivery; Agents and analysts co-execute with maker-checker controls and full source traceability; Critic, validator and governance agents at each decision point; Natural entry for existing managed-services clients; platform priced as an uplift on analyst fees; Two acquisitions in 18 months to deepen engineering and AI capability. Vendor-claimed metrics (unaudited): Domain analysts: 6,000+; Clients: 700+; Accuracy on complex financial queries: 95%+; Revenue invested in AI and technology: about 15%. Partners: Microsoft Azure, AWS, Databricks, Snowflake, LangChain. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 33, 34.

chunks.title: Agilisium
chunks.text: Agilisium, founded 2014, headquartered in Los Angeles, United States. AIM Research 2026 PeMa Quadrant: Leaders. Penetration score 0.66 (rank 5 of 28), Maturity score 0.56 (rank 15 of 28). Focus: Life sciences specialist embedding GenAI across R&D, clinical, regulatory, medical and commercial operations with compliance-first architectures. Industries: Life sciences and pharmaceuticals, Media and entertainment, Manufacturing, CPG. Markets: North America, Europe, Asia Pacific. Named platforms and accelerators: GenInsights Platform (Unified GenAI platform for querying, document intelligence and insight); Doc Sonar (Clinical and regulatory document intelligence); Pharma Rep Co-Pilot (Sales enablement with next-best-action); Sales Forecast AI (Data Detective) (Agentic commercial forecasting); Omnichannel Observability (Cross-channel customer journey analytics). Differentiators: Domain-trained embeddings and SME-led model development; Agentic workflows in regulated processes such as MLR review and biomarker analysis; Controls built in for 21 CFR Part 11, HIPAA, FDA and EMA obligations; 25+ prebuilt solutions across the pharma value chain; Innovation Labs and co-innovation model. Vendor-claimed metrics (unaudited): POC to production: Often within weeks; Prebuilt GenAI solutions: 25+. Partners: AWS, Microsoft Azure, Databricks, Snowflake, Salesforce. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 35, 36.

chunks.title: Akaike Technologies
chunks.text: Akaike Technologies, founded 2018, headquartered in Bengaluru, India. AIM Research 2026 PeMa Quadrant: Challengers. Penetration score 0.15 (rank 27 of 28), Maturity score 0.25 (rank 26 of 28). Focus: Pharma and life sciences regulated workflows such as dossier authoring and competitive intelligence, plus multimodal content across voice, video and text. Industries: Pharma and life sciences, Retail and CPG, Media and entertainment, Manufacturing, BFSI. Markets: United States, India. Named platforms and accelerators: Regulatory Content Automation Platform (Compliant dossier authoring at scale); Competitive Intelligence Engine (Real-time monitoring of regulatory, payer and competitor data); AI Video Studio (Script-to-video generation); Multimodal Ingestion Engine (High-throughput text, image and audio pipelines); Semantic Context Layer (Knowledge-graph and schema foundation for grounding); Agent ML (Automated ML lifecycle). Differentiators: Multimodal depth including voice cloning and AI video; Hybrid retrieval with adaptive chunking; Semantic layer to reduce hallucination; Evaluation stack with RAG metrics, LLM-as-judge and adversarial testing; GxP and GDPR alignment on AWS-native infrastructure. Partners: AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 37, 38.

chunks.title: Aspire Systems
chunks.text: Aspire Systems, founded 1996, headquartered in Chennai, India. AIM Research 2026 PeMa Quadrant: Growth Vendors. Penetration score 0.53 (rank 11 of 28), Maturity score 0.44 (rank 21 of 28). Focus: Knowledge assistants for any function, document intelligence and automated customer support, with particular depth in education and retail, delivered through a lifecycle platform. Industries: Education, Engineering and construction, Manufacturing. Markets: United States, Asia Pacific, EMEA. Named platforms and accelerators: Pragma (Dev, Data and Ops lifecycle platform for agents); Reusable RAG Framework (Ingestion, embedding, retrieval and evaluation pipelines); Prompt and Evaluation Accelerator (Prompt libraries with testing and benchmarking); Agent Orchestration Framework (Modular agents driven by a workflow engine); Domain Starter Kits (Edtech and retail templates); LLMOps Monitoring Dashboard (Performance, cost, safety and usage observability). Benefit and status: Improve efficiency and productivity, today: 66%; Improve efficiency and productivity, hoped: 60%; Enhance decision-making, today: 53%; Enhance decision-making, hoped: 61%; Reduce costs, today: 40%; Reduce costs, hoped: 65%; Enhance customer relationships, today: 38%; Enhance customer relationships, hoped: 60%; Improve products and innovation, today: 38%; Improve products and innovation, hoped: 60%; Increase revenue, today: 20%; Increase revenue, hoped: 74%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 10.

chunks.title: Depth of AI transformation
chunks.text: Depth of AI transformation. Approach: Deep transformation of products, processes or business model: 34%; Redesigning key processes around AI: 30%; Surface use, little or no process change: 37%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Note: Sums to 101 from rounding. Source footer prints N as 3,325, a typo. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 11.

chunks.title: Expect at least 10% of jobs to be fully automated
chunks.text: Expect at least 10% of jobs to be fully automated. Horizon: Within one year: 36%; Within three years: 82%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: Organisations that have not redesigned jobs around AI
chunks.text: Organisations that have not redesigned jobs around AI: 84%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 13.

chunks.title: Flatter or pod-based organisational structures
chunks.text: Flatter or pod-based organisational structures. Status: Considered: 53%; Adopted to a great or maximum extent: 16%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 13.

chunks.title: Non-technical worker sentiment toward AI, as reported by leaders
chunks.text: Non-technical worker sentiment toward AI, as reported by leaders. Sentiment: Highly enthusiastic: 13%; Open to exploring: 55%; Would rather not but will if required: 21%; Actively distrust and avoid: 4%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 14.

chunks.title: Talent strategy adjustments made because of AI
chunks.text: Talent strategy adjustments made because of AI. Adjustment: Educating the workforce to raise AI fluency: 53%; Upskilling and reskilling strategies: 48%; Hiring specialised AI talent: 36%; Redesigning career paths: 33%; Assessing future skills supply and demand: 30%; Incentives for using AI: 30%; Reorganising around new work patterns: 30%; Measuring worker trust and engagement: 30%; Changing full-time, contract and gig mix: 19%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 14.

chunks.title: Importance of data residency and local compute in strategic planning
chunks.text: Importance of data residency and local compute in strategic planning. Rating: Very important: 43%; Moderately important: 40%; Slightly important: 15%; Not at all important: 3%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Note: 83% at least moderately important. Sums to 101 from rounding. chunks.title: Concern about reliance on foreign-owned AI technology and compute
chunks.text: Concern about reliance on foreign-owned AI technology and compute. Rating: Very concerned: 22%; Moderately concerned: 44%; Slightly concerned: 24%; Not concerned: 10%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Note: 66% at least moderately concerned. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 15.

chunks.title: Organisations that weigh an AI solution's country of origin in vendor selection
chunks.text: Organisations that weigh an AI solution's country of origin in vendor selection: 77%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 5, 16.

chunks.title: Organisations building their AI stack mainly with local vendors
chunks.text: Organisations building their AI stack mainly with local vendors: 58%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 16.

chunks.title: Organisations sourcing the majority of their AI stack from foreign vendors, by region
chunks.text: Organisations sourcing the majority of their AI stack from foreign vendors, by region. Region: Americas: 11%; EMEA: 32%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 16.

chunks.title: Extent of agentic AI use, today vs in two years
chunks.text: Extent of agentic AI use, today vs in two years. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 17.

chunks.title: Organisations using agentic AI at least moderately
chunks.text: Organisations using agentic AI at least moderately. Horizon: Today: 23%; Expected in two years: 74%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 6, 17.

chunks.title: Organisations expecting to customise AI agents to their business
chunks.text: Organisations expecting to customise AI agents to their business: 85%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 18.

chunks.title: Organisations with a mature governance model for autonomous agents
chunks.text: Organisations with a mature governance model for autonomous agents: 21%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 6, 20.

chunks.title: AI risks organisations are most concerned about
chunks.text: AI risks organisations are most concerned about. Risk: Data privacy and security: 73%; Legal, IP or regulatory compliance: 50%; Governance capability and oversight: 46%; Model quality, consistency and explainability: 46%; Workforce impact: 30%; Other or no concerns: 0%. Sample: 3,199 respondents. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 21.

chunks.title: Organisations using physical AI at least to a limited extent
chunks.text: Organisations using physical AI at least to a limited extent. Horizon: Today: 58%; Expected in two years: 80%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Note: Physical AI covers robotics, drones, automated machinery and digital twins. Of the companies using it today, 18% do so at a moderate or greater level. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 6, 22.

chunks.title: Physical AI use by region, today vs in two years
chunks.text: Physical AI use by region, today vs in two years. Region and horizon: Americas, today: 56%; Americas, in 2 years: 77%; EMEA, today: 56%; EMEA, in 2 years: 81%; Asia Pacific, today: 71%; Asia Pacific, in 2 years: 90%. Sample: EMEA 1,170; Asia Pacific 475; the caption gives the Americas base as 3,235, which is the full sample, so the Americas base is probably the remaining 1,590 or so (our estimate). Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 23.

chunks.title: Types of physical AI expected to have the greatest impact
chunks.text: Types of physical AI expected to have the greatest impact. Type: Intelligent security and smart monitoring: 21%; Collaborative robotics: 20%; Digital twins: 19%; IoT-driven retail: 16%; Autonomous logistics: 13%; Smart materials: 7%; Other: 3%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Note: Sums to 99 from rounding. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 25.

chunks.title: Organisations rating themselves highly prepared for AI adoption, by dimension
chunks.text: Organisations rating themselves highly prepared for AI adoption, by dimension. Dimension: Technology infrastructure: 43%; Strategy: 42%; Data management: 40%; Risk and governance: 30%; Talent: 20%. Sample: 3,235 leaders, 24 countries, Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise, fielded Aug to Sep 2025. Note: Change vs prior year: -4, +3, -3, +6, -2 points respectively. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 28.

chunks.text: Full AI preparedness distribution, by dimension. Dimension and level: Technology infrastructure, not prepared: 1%; Technology infrastructure, slightly: 14%; Technology infrastructure, moderately: 42%; Technology infrastructure, highly: 43%; Strategy, not prepared: 3%; Strategy, slightly: 15%; Strategy, moderately: 41%; Strategy, highly: 42%; Data management, not prepared: 2%; Data management, slightly: 14%; Data management, moderately: 44%; Data management, highly: 40%; Risk and governance, not prepared: 5%; Risk and governance, slightly: 22%; Risk and governance, moderately: 42%; Risk and governance, highly: 30%; Talent, not prepared: 6%; Talent, slightly: 29%; Talent, moderately: 45%; Talent, highly: 20%. chunks.title: KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026 survey sample
chunks.text: KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026 survey sample: 204. Note: US C-suite and business leaders at organisations with $1B+ revenue. The report does not say whether the same firms answer each quarter. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 3.

chunks.text: Average projected AI investment over the next 12 months, by quarter (USD millions). Quarter: Q2 2025: 88; Q3 2025: 130; Q4 2025: 124; Q1 2026: 207; Q2 2026: 202. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Note: Average of projected spend; a few very large answers can move it. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 3.

chunks.title: Planning to invest $10M to $49M by category
chunks.text: Planning to invest $10M to $49M by category. Category: Cybersecurity: 55%; Data and analytics: 48%; Research and development: 45%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 3.

chunks.title: Leaders who agree their AI strategy is future-proof
chunks.text: Leaders who agree their AI strategy is future-proof: 66%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Note: Able to adapt to new technology and regulation, scale responsibly and avoid vendor lock-in. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 3.

chunks.title: Top factors expected to influence AI strategy in the next six months
chunks.text: Top factors expected to influence AI strategy in the next six months. Factor: Data security, privacy and risk: 92%; Pressure to show value to investors or board: 76%; Limits on hiring and upskilling: 68%; Access to lower-cost, high-fidelity models: 68%; Balancing AI scale with carbon and sustainability: 68%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 3.

chunks.text: What triggers a decision to override an AI output. Trigger: Output conflicts with regulatory or legal requirements: 47%; Confidence or quality scores below limits: 43%; Case by case, no formal criteria: 33%; Business judgment differs from the recommendation: 29%; Predefined risk thresholds exceeded: 29%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 4.

chunks.title: Who is accountable for AI-informed or AI-executed business decisions
chunks.text: Who is accountable for AI-informed or AI-executed business decisions. Owner: A named C-suite executive (CIO, CAIO, COO): 34%; CEO or executive committee: 32%; Business unit leader: 14%; Central AI governance or risk committee: 10%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 4.

chunks.title: Leaders who agree their CEO actively owns AI as a strategic priority
chunks.text: Leaders who agree their CEO actively owns AI as a strategic priority: 67%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 4.

chunks.title: Top planned risk control for AI agents is output-level human-in-the-loop validation
chunks.text: Top planned risk control for AI agents is output-level human-in-the-loop validation: 52%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Note: A person validates outputs without overseeing each agent action. Top answer for the second consecutive quarter. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 4.

chunks.title: Organisations whose AI operating costs are fully visible today
chunks.text: Organisations whose AI operating costs are fully visible today: 26%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 5.

chunks.title: AI cost controls currently in place
chunks.text: AI cost controls currently in place. Control: AI cost monitoring dashboards: 66%; Cost review within the AI approval process: 61%; Architecture or prompt design standards: 47%; Usage or token budgets: 36%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 5.

chunks.title: AI agent deployment rate among large US firms
chunks.text: AI agent deployment rate among large US firms. Quarter: Q1 2026: 55%; Q2 2026: 53%. Sample: Q2 2026: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026; the Q1 value comes from the prior wave, whose sample this report does not state. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 6.

chunks.title: Stage of AI agent adoption, Q1 vs Q2 2026
chunks.text: Stage of AI agent adoption, Q1 vs Q2 2026. Stage and quarter: Scaling agents across functions, Q1: 33%; Scaling agents across functions, Q2: 29%; Orchestrating agents across workflows, Q1: 9%; Orchestrating agents across workflows, Q2: 18%; Building multi-agent systems, Q1: 6%; Building multi-agent systems, Q2: 6%; Piloting agents, Q1: 30%; Piloting agents, Q2: 35%; Exploring agents, Q1: 14%; Exploring agents, Q2: 10%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Note: Q1 stages sum to 48% deployed against a stated 55% deployment rate; Q2 stages reconcile. An unlabelled remainder exists. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 6.

chunks.title: How AI agents support collaboration across functions
chunks.text: How AI agents support collaboration across functions. Use: Aligning shared goals, KPIs and success metrics: 64%; Supporting joint decision-making: 49%; Automating workflows that span functions: 48%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 6.

chunks.text: Biggest challenges to deploying AI agents. Challenge: Data readiness and access: 58%; Human oversight skills: 43%; Complexity of agentic systems: 38%; Technical skills gaps: 37%; AI cost and economic literacy: 35%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 6.

chunks.title: Employee response to AI agents, Q2 2026
chunks.text: Employee response to AI agents, Q2 2026. Response: Some level of adoption: 43%; Mixed response: 37%; Slight resistance: 19%; Significant resistance: 1%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 7.

chunks.title: Employee adoption of AI agents, quarter over quarter
chunks.text: Employee adoption of AI agents, quarter over quarter. Quarter: Q1 2026: 55%; Q2 2026: 43%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 7.

chunks.text: Employee resistance to AI agents, quarter over quarter. Quarter: Q1 2026: 5%; Q2 2026: 20%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 7.

chunks.title: Resistance driven by added workload or complexity, quarter over quarter
chunks.text: Resistance driven by added workload or complexity, quarter over quarter. Quarter: Q1 2026: 28%; Q2 2026: 51%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 7.

chunks.title: Employee concerns about AI, Q1 vs Q2 2026
chunks.text: Employee concerns about AI, Q1 vs Q2 2026. Concern and quarter: Skills gaps, Q1: 76%; Skills gaps, Q2: 57%; Insufficient training or support, Q1: 53%; Insufficient training or support, Q2: 27%; Job security, Q1: 67%; Job security, Q2: 55%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 7.

chunks.title: Leaders who agree strong AI users are outperforming other employees
chunks.text: Leaders who agree strong AI users are outperforming other employees: 47%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 7.

chunks.title: Leaders who would consider token-maxxing incentives
chunks.text: Leaders who would consider token-maxxing incentives: 41%. Sample: 204 US C-suite and business leaders at $1B+ firms, KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse Q2 2026, fielded 28 Apr to 25 May 2026. Note: Rewarding employees for consuming as many tokens as possible, often via leaderboards. KPMG warns usage-based incentives can reward the wrong behaviour. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 2, 7.

chunks.title: Menlo Ventures 2025 survey sample
chunks.text: Menlo Ventures 2025 survey sample: 495. Note: US enterprise AI decision-makers at companies already using AI, fielded 7 to 25 November 2025, combined with a bottom-up market model. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Enterprise generative AI spend by year (USD billions)
chunks.text: Enterprise generative AI spend by year (USD billions). Year: 2022: 0; 2023: 1.7; 2024: 11.5; 2025: 37.0. Sample: 495 US enterprise AI decision-makers, Menlo Ventures, 7 to 25 Nov 2025, plus Menlo's market-sizing model. Note: Menlo's spend series excludes chips, inference and model serving, and AI features bundled into existing software. 2023 and 2024 restated to remove inference. Growth 6.8x in 2024 and 3.2x in 2025; about 6% of a roughly $300B SaaS market. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Generative AI spend by category, 2023 to 2025 (USD billions)
chunks.text: Generative AI spend by category, 2023 to 2025 (USD billions). Category and year: Foundation model APIs 2023: 0.5; Foundation model APIs 2024: 3.5; Foundation model APIs 2025: 12.5; Model training 2023: 0.5; Model training 2024: 3.0; Model training 2025: 4.0; AI infrastructure 2023: 0.1; AI infrastructure 2024: 0.4; AI infrastructure 2025: 1.5; Horizontal AI 2023: 0.3; Horizontal AI 2024: 1.6; Horizontal AI 2025: 8.4; Departmental AI 2023: 0.2; Departmental AI 2024: 1.8; Departmental AI 2025: 7.3; Vertical AI 2023: 0.1; Vertical AI 2024: 1.2; Vertical AI 2025: 3.5. Sample: 495 US enterprise AI decision-makers, Menlo Ventures, 7 to 25 Nov 2025, plus Menlo's market-sizing model. Note: Infrastructure $18B and applications $19B in 2025. Growth 2024 to 2025: 3.6x, 1.3x, 3.8x, 5.3x, 4.1x, 2.9x. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: AI use cases purchased vs built in-house
chunks.text: AI use cases purchased vs built in-house. Method and year: Purchased, 2024: 53%; Built internally, 2024: 47%; Purchased, 2025: 76%; Built internally, 2025: 24%. Sample: 495 US enterprise AI decision-makers, Menlo Ventures, 7 to 25 Nov 2025, plus Menlo's market-sizing model. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Pilot-to-production funnel, AI purchases vs traditional software
chunks.text: Pilot-to-production funnel, AI purchases vs traditional software. Sample: 495 US enterprise AI decision-makers, Menlo Ventures, 7 to 25 Nov 2025, plus Menlo's market-sizing model. Note: Measures purchased solutions, not internal builds. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Product-led growth share of AI application spend vs traditional software
chunks.text: Product-led growth share of AI application spend vs traditional software. Category: AI applications: 27%; Traditional software: 7%. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.text: Startup share of AI application revenue. Year: 2024: 36%; 2025: 63%. Sample: 495 US enterprise AI decision-makers, Menlo Ventures, 7 to 25 Nov 2025, plus Menlo's market-sizing model. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.text: Startup vs incumbent revenue share by layer, 2025. chunks.text: Startup share of departmental AI revenue, by department. chunks.text: Departmental AI spend by department, 2025 (USD millions). chunks.text: Vertical AI spend by industry, 2025 (USD millions). chunks.text: Enterprise LLM API share by vendor, 2023 to 2025 (Menlo estimate). chunks.title: Generative AI (GenAI)
chunks.text: Generative AI (GenAI): AI systems, usually built on large language models, that produce text, code, images or other content from prompts. In enterprises it now spans assistive tools such as copilots through to autonomous agents. Related terms: LLM, Agentic AI, Copilot. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6, 15.

chunks.title: LLM
chunks.text: LLM (Large Language Model): A neural network trained on very large text corpora that can understand and generate language. Agents use LLMs as their reasoning engine. Related terms: Generative AI (GenAI), Agentic AI, Model routing. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: Agentic AI
chunks.text: Agentic AI: AI systems in which agents, powered by LLMs, plan multi-step tasks, call tools and APIs, validate their own outputs and trigger actions in enterprise systems with limited human direction. Both sources treat it as the current frontier of enterprise AI. Related terms: AI agent, Multi-agent orchestration, Agentic RAG, MCP. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 6, 15; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 4, 11; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 17; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 6; Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: AI agent
chunks.text: AI agent: A software component that uses an LLM to decide what to do next, can invoke tools, keep state or memory, and act on other systems. Several agents working together form a multi-agent system. Related terms: Agentic AI, Multi-agent orchestration, AgentOps. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 5, 12; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 6; Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Multi-agent orchestration
chunks.text: Multi-agent orchestration: Coordinating several specialised agents (for example planner, extractor, validator, publisher) so they complete a workflow together. Increasingly the default approach to complex automation, though scaled production examples remain a minority. Related terms: Agentic AI, A2A, MCP, AgentOps. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6, 13; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 12; KPMG US, 2026, pages 6.

chunks.title: Copilot
chunks.text: Copilot: An assistive AI application that helps a person do their job, such as drafting, summarising or answering questions, while the person stays in control. The first wave of enterprise GenAI was dominated by copilots. Related terms: Assistive and embedded workloads, Agentic AI. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 13; Menlo Ventures, 2025; Microsoft, 2026, pages 8.

chunks.title: Assistive and embedded workloads
chunks.text: Assistive and embedded workloads: AIM's family of GenAI work where the model helps a person or is embedded in an existing system: content generation, knowledge retrieval (RAG), model customisation and multimodal processing. Related terms: Agentic and orchestrated workloads, RAG, Copilot. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 15, 18.

chunks.title: Agentic and orchestrated workloads
chunks.text: Agentic and orchestrated workloads: AIM's second family of GenAI work: multi-step tasks executed with planning, tool use and workflow automation. The fastest-growing segment. Related terms: Assistive and embedded workloads, Agentic AI. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 15, 18.

chunks.title: RAG
chunks.text: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): An architecture where the system first retrieves relevant enterprise documents or data, then gives them to the LLM so its answer is grounded in that content. Now considered table stakes; the first pattern most enterprises adopt. Related terms: Agentic RAG, Hybrid search, Chunking, Vector database, Embedding, Knowledge graph. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6, 12, 15; Menlo Ventures, 2025; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 207.

chunks.title: Agentic RAG
chunks.text: Agentic RAG: A RAG pattern in which retrieval, reasoning and action are orchestrated dynamically by an agent rather than in a fixed pipeline. Named as a differentiator once basic RAG is commoditised. Related terms: RAG, Agentic AI. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6.

chunks.title: Hybrid search
chunks.text: Hybrid search: Combining vector (semantic) search with keyword search and a re-ranking step to improve retrieval quality in RAG systems. Related terms: RAG, Re-ranking, Vector database. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: Re-ranking
chunks.text: Re-ranking: A second-stage model that re-orders retrieved passages by relevance before they are passed to the LLM. Related terms: Hybrid search, RAG. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: Chunking
chunks.text: Chunking: Splitting documents into passages for indexing and retrieval. Domain-specific chunking strategies are cited as a source of RAG quality differences. Related terms: RAG, Embedding. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6, 12.

chunks.title: Embedding
chunks.text: Embedding: A numeric vector representing the meaning of a piece of text (or image) so that similar items can be found by distance. Domain-specific embedding models are used to improve retrieval in specialised fields. Related terms: Vector database, RAG. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: Vector database
chunks.text: Vector database: A datastore optimised for storing embeddings and finding nearest neighbours, used as the retrieval layer in RAG. Related terms: Embedding, RAG. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12, 23.

chunks.title: Knowledge graph
chunks.text: Knowledge graph: A structured network of entities and relationships that gives an LLM explicit facts and context. Used to augment RAG and reduce hallucination. Related terms: Semantic layer, RAG. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6, 12.

chunks.title: Semantic layer
chunks.text: Semantic layer: A layer that maps enterprise data, business rules, glossary terms and context into a form agents and LLMs can use consistently. Also called an enterprise context layer or ontology. Related terms: Knowledge graph, RAG. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12, 23.

chunks.title: Document intelligence
chunks.text: Document intelligence: Pipelines that ingest documents, apply OCR, classify, extract fields and enrich metadata so unstructured content becomes usable by AI and downstream systems. Related terms: RAG, Multimodal AI. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: Multimodal AI
chunks.text: Multimodal AI: Models and pipelines that reason across text, images, audio and video, for example OCR plus LLM document digitisation. Related terms: Document intelligence. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12, 15.

chunks.title: Fine-tuning
chunks.text: Fine-tuning: Further training a foundation model on domain data so it performs better on specific tasks or language. Techniques include LoRA, QLoRA, RLHF and DPO. Related terms: LoRA / QLoRA, RLHF, DPO, Domain model adaptation. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12, 23; Menlo Ventures, 2025; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: LoRA / QLoRA
chunks.text: LoRA / QLoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation / Quantised LoRA): Efficient fine-tuning methods that train a small set of extra parameters instead of the whole model, cutting cost and memory. Related terms: Fine-tuning. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: RLHF
chunks.text: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback): A training method that uses human preference judgements to steer model behaviour. Related terms: Fine-tuning, DPO. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: DPO
chunks.text: DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation): A simpler alternative to RLHF that optimises the model directly on preference pairs. Related terms: Fine-tuning, RLHF. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: Domain model adaptation
chunks.text: Domain model adaptation: Adapting models to an industry's language and accuracy needs through fine-tuning, custom embeddings, prompt optimisation and domain evaluation sets. Deployed selectively where accuracy is business-critical. Related terms: Fine-tuning, Embedding. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 15.

chunks.title: Prompt engineering
chunks.text: Prompt engineering: Designing and tuning the instructions given to an LLM, including structured prompts, prompt libraries, versioning and automated optimisation. Related terms: Prompt compression, LLMOps. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12, 20; Menlo Ventures, 2025; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 207.

chunks.title: Prompt compression
chunks.text: Prompt compression: Reducing the number of tokens sent to a model without losing meaning, to lower cost and latency. Related terms: Prompt engineering, Caching (context and response), Model routing. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 10, 20.

chunks.title: Model routing
chunks.text: Model routing: Sending each request to the cheapest model that can handle it, reserving large models for complex reasoning. A core cost-control technique. Related terms: Prompt compression, Caching (context and response), FinOps. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 10, 12, 20, 50; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: Caching (context and response)
chunks.text: Caching (context and response): Reusing previously computed prompt context or answers so repeated requests cost fewer tokens. Related terms: Model routing, Prompt compression. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 10, 20.

chunks.title: Guardrails
chunks.text: Guardrails: Controls that constrain model inputs and outputs: prompt-injection and jailbreak defence, content moderation, PII redaction, bias and hallucination checks. Related terms: Prompt injection, Hallucination, Red-teaming. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12, 13, 20.

chunks.title: Prompt injection
chunks.text: Prompt injection: An attack where malicious text in the input or in retrieved content makes the model ignore its instructions. Input validation against it is part of LLMOps. Related terms: Guardrails, Jailbreak. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13.

chunks.title: Jailbreak
chunks.text: Jailbreak: A prompt crafted to bypass a model's safety behaviour. Jailbreak prevention is listed alongside prompt-injection defence. Related terms: Prompt injection, Guardrails. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13.

chunks.title: Red-teaming
chunks.text: Red-teaming: Deliberate adversarial testing of a model or agent to find failure modes before deployment. Related terms: Guardrails, Evaluation-driven development. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12, 54, 58.

chunks.title: Hallucination
chunks.text: Hallucination: A confident but false or unsupported model output. The failure mode that does the most damage to buyer confidence, worse in production than in controlled pilots. Related terms: RAG, Citation enforcement, Confidence scoring, Human-in-the-loop (HITL), Evaluation-driven development. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 9.

chunks.title: Citation enforcement
chunks.text: Citation enforcement: Requiring the model to attach source references to its statements so outputs are traceable to documents. A common response to hallucination in regulated settings. Related terms: Hallucination, RAG. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 9, 72.

chunks.title: Confidence scoring
chunks.text: Confidence scoring: Attaching a confidence estimate to each output so low-confidence answers can be routed to human review. Related terms: Hallucination, Human-in-the-loop (HITL). Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 9, 42.

chunks.title: Human-in-the-loop (HITL)
chunks.text: Human-in-the-loop (HITL): Design pattern where a person reviews, approves or corrects AI outputs at defined checkpoints. Used both to manage risk and to build user trust incrementally. Cited by 33 percent of IDC respondents as a top barrier to scaling agents. Related terms: Hallucination, Confidence scoring, Maker-checker. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 9, 20; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 12; KPMG US, 2026, pages 4; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 19.

chunks.title: Maker-checker
chunks.text: Maker-checker: A control in which one party produces an output and a second independently checks it before it is accepted. Applied to agent and analyst workflows in regulated finance. Related terms: Human-in-the-loop (HITL), Critic or evaluator agent. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 34.

chunks.title: Critic or evaluator agent
chunks.text: Critic or evaluator agent: An agent whose job is to check another agent's output for factuality, citation completeness or policy compliance and grade its confidence. Related terms: LLM-as-a-judge, Multi-agent orchestration. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12, 33.

chunks.title: LLM-as-a-judge
chunks.text: LLM-as-a-judge: Using a language model to score the quality of another model's outputs at scale, as part of an evaluation framework. Related terms: Evaluation-driven development, Critic or evaluator agent. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 38.

chunks.title: Evaluation-driven development
chunks.text: Evaluation-driven development: Building GenAI systems with automated quality benchmarks and ground-truth test sets embedded through the build cycle and kept running in production, rather than one-time testing. A trait of vendors with high pilot-to-production conversion. Related terms: LLM-as-a-judge, LLMOps, Drift detection. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 6, 9.

chunks.title: LLMOps
chunks.text: LLMOps: The operational discipline for GenAI systems: CI/CD with prompt and model versioning, monitoring, drift and hallucination tracking, cost and token control, security and audit logging. Described as the layer where production viability is decided. Related terms: AgentOps, MLOps, FinOps, Drift detection, Observability. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 7, 13, 20.

chunks.title: MLOps
chunks.text: MLOps: The established practice of deploying and operating machine-learning models; LLMOps extends it for language models and AgentOps for agents. Related terms: LLMOps, AgentOps. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13, 23.

chunks.title: AgentOps
chunks.text: AgentOps: Monitoring, governance and lifecycle management specific to AI agents: tracing agent actions, enforcing policies, evaluating behaviour and controlling execution. Related terms: LLMOps, Observability. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13, 56.

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.text: Observability: End-to-end visibility into a GenAI pipeline: tokens, cost, latency, accuracy and agent traces, with feedback loops into improvement. Related terms: LLMOps, AgentOps, Drift detection. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20.

chunks.title: Drift detection
chunks.text: Drift detection: Detecting when model behaviour, data or retrieval quality changes over time so systems can be retrained or retuned. Related terms: LLMOps, Observability. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13, 20.

chunks.title: FinOps
chunks.text: FinOps: Financial operations discipline applied to cloud and AI spend: real-time cost tracking, budgets and optimisation. Named as a required control for production GenAI. Related terms: Model routing, LLMOps. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 7, 59, 83; KPMG US, 2026, pages 5; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 19.

chunks.title: SRE discipline
chunks.text: SRE discipline (Site Reliability Engineering): Running AI systems with the same reliability engineering rigour as other production services: SLAs, incident response, capacity and cost management. Related terms: LLMOps. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 7.

chunks.title: MCP
chunks.text: MCP (Model Context Protocol): An open protocol that standardises how agents connect to tools and data sources. Several vendors name MCP hosting or gateways in their agent platforms. Related terms: A2A, Tool calling, Multi-agent orchestration. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13, 43, 54, 83; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 18, 22.

chunks.title: A2A
chunks.text: A2A (Agent-to-Agent protocol): A protocol for agents built on different frameworks to discover and communicate with each other. Relevant to the barrier of managing agents across frameworks. Related terms: MCP, Multi-agent orchestration. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 12; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 18, 22.

chunks.title: Tool calling
chunks.text: Tool calling: The ability of an LLM or agent to invoke functions, APIs or enterprise systems as part of completing a task. Related terms: MCP, AI agent. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13; Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: ReAct
chunks.text: ReAct (Reason and Act): An agent reasoning loop that alternates between thinking about the next step and taking an action, then observing the result. One of the common agent design patterns alongside plan-and-execute and reflection. Related terms: AI agent, Plan-and-execute. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13, 65.

chunks.title: Plan-and-execute
chunks.text: Plan-and-execute: An agent pattern that first produces a full plan and then executes its steps, in contrast to ReAct's step-by-step loop. Reflection adds a self-review step. Related terms: ReAct, AI agent. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13.

chunks.title: Text-to-SQL
chunks.text: Text-to-SQL: Turning a natural-language question into a database query so business users can ask questions of structured data. Underpins conversational BI products. Related terms: Conversational BI. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13, 67, 72.

chunks.title: Conversational BI
chunks.text: Conversational BI (Conversational Business Intelligence): Natural-language interfaces over dashboards and data warehouses that answer questions and generate narrative insights. Related terms: Text-to-SQL, Copilot. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 18, 43, 69.

chunks.title: Synthetic personas and audiences
chunks.text: Synthetic personas and audiences: Simulated customer segments generated by AI, used to test product concepts, messaging or pricing before real-market research. An emerging product category among service providers. Related terms: Synthetic data. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13, 43, 45.

chunks.title: Synthetic data
chunks.text: Synthetic data: Artificially generated data used for training, testing or privacy-preserving analysis. Related terms: Synthetic personas and audiences. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: Digital twin
chunks.text: Digital twin: A virtual replica of a physical asset, site, process or network, used to simulate and test what-if scenarios. Some providers pair it with agents for risk and operations planning. Related terms: Control tower. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 31, 32; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 25.

chunks.title: Control tower
chunks.text: Control tower: A domain command centre that combines monitoring, prediction, agent recommendations and workflow execution, typically for supply chain or finance operations. Related terms: Digital twin. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 31, 65.

chunks.title: Accelerator
chunks.text: Accelerator: A reusable, pre-built asset a service provider brings to engagements: RAG kits, agent frameworks, evaluation libraries, dashboards, domain templates. Vendors typically disclose 5 to 10; most are point solutions rather than integrated platforms. Related terms: Platform-led delivery. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 14.

chunks.title: Platform-led delivery
chunks.text: Platform-led delivery: A delivery model built around a vendor's own integrated platform rather than bespoke builds. Vendors with individually named platform components show higher productisation maturity. Related terms: Accelerator. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 7.

chunks.title: Centre of Excellence (CoE)
chunks.text: Centre of Excellence (CoE): A central team that standardises practices, maintains reusable assets and drives adoption of AI across an organisation, whether inside an enterprise or a service provider. Related terms: Accelerator. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12, 20, 34.

chunks.title: Forward-deployed engineer
chunks.text: Forward-deployed engineer: An engineer who works inside the client's environment to turn business needs into deployable solutions, bridging technical and business teams. Associated with better pilot-to-production conversion. Related terms: Co-creation. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 23.

chunks.title: Co-creation
chunks.text: Co-creation: Building solutions jointly with the client, in their environment, on their data and platforms, iterating toward production. Cited as improving adoption and continuity. Related terms: Forward-deployed engineer, Co-innovation. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 19, 69.

chunks.title: Co-innovation
chunks.text: Co-innovation: A joint development engagement model used for strategic or complex initiatives, also used for vendor-to-platform partnerships. Related terms: Co-creation, Engagement model. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 22, 44.

chunks.title: POC-to-production gap
chunks.text: POC-to-production gap (Proof of Concept to production): The drop-off between GenAI pilots and systems that reach governed production use. Named the defining fault line of the market: most vendors convert 25 to 45 percent of pilots and industry pilot failure exceeds 70 percent. Causes are mostly organisational (governance, talent, change, compliance) rather than model quality. Related terms: Change management and adoption, Data readiness, Micro POC. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 6, 9; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 8, 9; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 6, 7; Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Micro POC
chunks.text: Micro POC: USEReady's name for a short proof of concept (two to four weeks), offered alongside fixed-price terms, that tests value before a client commits to scale. Related terms: POC-to-production gap. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 83, 84.

chunks.title: Data readiness
chunks.text: Data readiness: Whether enterprise data is clean, consistent, documented and context-rich enough for GenAI. The gap between data that exists and data that is RAG-ready is the largest technical friction point, and data quality is the top technical challenge in the IDC survey. Related terms: RAG, POC-to-production gap, Real-time data. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 9; IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 13; KPMG US, 2026, pages 6; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 13.

chunks.title: Change management and adoption
chunks.text: Change management and adoption: The organisational work of getting people to trust and use AI systems: workflow embedding, role-based enablement, incremental trust building. Broadly under-invested; adoption failure is called the primary ROI risk. Related terms: POC-to-production gap, Human-in-the-loop (HITL). Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 7, 9; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 14; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 11.

chunks.title: Engagement model
chunks.text: Engagement model: The commercial structure of a services contract: project-based, capacity-led (pods), run-and-operate (managed services), outcome-linked, platform subscription, or co-innovation. Related terms: Outcome-linked pricing, Managed services (run and operate), Time and materials (T&M). Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 22.

chunks.title: Time and materials (T&M)
chunks.text: Time and materials (T&M): Billing by effort and hours rather than by fixed scope or outcome. Still the default for most GenAI engagements. Related terms: Engagement model, Outcome-linked pricing. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 22.

chunks.title: Outcome-linked pricing
chunks.text: Outcome-linked pricing: Tying part of a vendor's fee to measured business results. Rare but rising; only a few vendors in the AIM study offer it. Related terms: Engagement model, Time and materials (T&M). Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 22, 44, 70.

chunks.title: Managed services (run and operate)
chunks.text: Managed services (run and operate): Ongoing operation of deployed AI systems by the vendor: monitoring, prompt tuning, knowledge refresh, retraining, support. The fastest-growing engagement model as production deployments increase. Related terms: Engagement model, LLMOps. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13, 22.

chunks.title: KPO
chunks.text: KPO (Knowledge Process Outsourcing): Outsourced analyst and research work. Vendors with KPO roots tend to keep large standing benches of domain specialists who now work alongside agents. Related terms: Domain SME bench. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 24, 34.

chunks.title: Domain SME bench
chunks.text: Domain SME bench (Subject Matter Expert bench): A large standing pool of industry specialists who take part in fine-tuning, output validation and quality assurance. One of two models for bringing domain expertise into delivery; the other draws SMEs from a shared pool as needed. Related terms: KPO, Human-in-the-loop (HITL). Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 24.

chunks.title: PeMa Quadrant
chunks.text: PeMa Quadrant (Penetration Maturity Quadrant): AIM Research's vendor evaluation framework. Vendors are scored 0 to 1 on Penetration (market reach) and Maturity (delivery depth) and placed into four quadrants: Leaders, Seasoned Vendors, Growth Vendors, Challengers. Related terms: Penetration (Pe), Maturity (Ma). Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 26, 27, 28.

chunks.title: Penetration (Pe)
chunks.text: Penetration (Pe): AIM's market-reach axis: delivery scale, financial health, growth, customer confidence, client reach and partnerships. Related terms: PeMa Quadrant, Maturity (Ma). Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 26.

chunks.title: Maturity (Ma)
chunks.text: Maturity (Ma): AIM's capability axis: work delivery, technical advancement, value realisation, team maturity and support infrastructure. Related terms: PeMa Quadrant, Penetration (Pe). Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 26.

chunks.title: Real-time data maturity tier
chunks.text: Real-time data maturity tier: IDC's four percentile groups (Emerging, Developing, Advanced, Leaders) based on a 0 to 100 composite of real-time deployment depth, agentic AI adoption and measurable outcomes. Related terms: Real-time data, Composite maturity score. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 7, 8.

chunks.title: Composite maturity score
chunks.text: Composite maturity score: IDC's 0 to 100 score per respondent. Tier averages: Emerging 35, Developing 50, Advanced 60, Leaders 74. Related terms: Real-time data maturity tier. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 8.

chunks.title: Real-time data
chunks.text: Real-time data: Data that is captured, moved and made available as events happen rather than in batches. IDC's survey finds it is now treated as core infrastructure for agentic AI. Related terms: Event-driven architecture, Unified real-time data platform, Real-time data maturity tier. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 4, 22.

chunks.title: Event-driven architecture
chunks.text: Event-driven architecture: A design in which systems publish and react to events (state changes) as they occur, typically through an event broker or mesh. The basis of real-time data platforms. Related terms: Real-time data, Unified real-time data platform. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 1, 22.

chunks.title: Unified real-time data platform
chunks.text: Unified real-time data platform: A single, integrated platform for real-time data instead of many loosely connected tools. IDC calls consolidation onto one the clearest marker of a leader: 71 percent of Leaders versus 8 percent of Emerging organisations. Related terms: Tool sprawl, Real-time data. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 15, 22.

chunks.title: Tool sprawl
chunks.text: Tool sprawl: An accumulation of overlapping, loosely integrated tools that raises complexity and cost. Cited by 37 percent of IDC respondents as a top technical challenge. Related terms: Unified real-time data platform, Legacy systems and technical debt. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 13, 15.

chunks.title: Legacy systems and technical debt
chunks.text: Legacy systems and technical debt: Older systems and accumulated shortcuts that make integration and real-time data harder. A top-five technical challenge for buyers and a recurring integration challenge for vendors. Related terms: Tool sprawl. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 13; AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 10.

chunks.title: AI success rate
chunks.text: AI success rate: In the IDC survey, the share of an organisation's AI projects that deliver measurable outcomes. Averages range from 34 percent (Emerging) to 67 percent (Leaders). Related terms: Real-time data maturity tier. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 8, 17, 18.

chunks.title: InfoBrief
chunks.text: InfoBrief: IDC's short, sponsored research format that presents survey findings for external distribution. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 1, 28.

chunks.title: BFSI
chunks.text: BFSI (Banking, Financial Services and Insurance): The industry grouping most often named by service providers as a focus and the deepest area of GenAI domain specialisation. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 5, 16.

chunks.title: CPG
chunks.text: CPG (Consumer Packaged Goods): Fast-moving consumer goods companies, frequently paired with retail in vendor focus areas. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 16.

chunks.title: Financial spreading
chunks.text: Financial spreading: Extracting figures from financial statements into a standard format for credit analysis. Several providers report production deployments of it for banks. Related terms: Document intelligence. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 16, 34, 49, 50.

chunks.title: DDQ
chunks.text: DDQ (Due Diligence Questionnaire): Standardised investor questionnaires whose drafting is a frequent GenAI use case in asset management. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 16, 72.

chunks.title: MLR review
chunks.text: MLR review (Medical, Legal, Regulatory review): The compliance review of pharmaceutical promotional content. Named as an agentic workflow in life sciences. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 16, 36.

chunks.title: Pharmacovigilance
chunks.text: Pharmacovigilance: Monitoring and assessing adverse drug effects. Cited as a reasoning-heavy workflow where multiple agents validate each other's outputs. Related terms: Multi-agent orchestration. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 76.

chunks.title: GxP and 21 CFR Part 11
chunks.text: GxP and 21 CFR Part 11 (Good Practice regulations; US FDA electronic records rule): Life-sciences quality and electronic-records regulations that GenAI systems in pharma must satisfy for validation, auditability and traceability. Related terms: HIPAA, SOC 2, GDPR. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 36, 37.

chunks.title: HIPAA, SOC 2, GDPR
chunks.text: HIPAA, SOC 2, GDPR: Common compliance standards (US health privacy, service-organisation security controls, EU data protection) that vendors cite as baseline requirements for production GenAI. Related terms: GxP and 21 CFR Part 11, PII detection and redaction. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20, 50.

chunks.title: PII detection and redaction
chunks.text: PII detection and redaction (Personally Identifiable Information): Automatically finding and masking personal data in inputs, outputs and training data, a standard governance control. Related terms: HIPAA, SOC 2, GDPR, Guardrails. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12, 13, 20.

chunks.title: RBAC
chunks.text: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): Restricting what each user or agent can see and do according to its role. Applied to agents as well as people in mature deployments. Related terms: Guardrails. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20, 34.

chunks.title: Small language model
chunks.text: Small language model: A compact model used for high-volume, lower-complexity tasks to cut cost and latency, with large models reserved for hard reasoning. Related terms: Model routing, LLM. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 50, 71; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 16.

chunks.title: Reasoning model
chunks.text: Reasoning model: A model trained to work through multi-step problems before answering. At least one service provider in the AIM study has released its own. Related terms: LLM. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 53, 54; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: Sovereign AI
chunks.text: Sovereign AI: Designing, training and running AI under a country's own laws, on infrastructure it controls, with locally governed data, so that critical capability does not depend on foreign vendors. In Deloitte's late-2025 survey of 3,235 leaders at AI-adopting organisations, 83% rated data residency and in-country compute at least moderately important to strategic planning, and 77% weighed an AI vendor's country of origin when choosing solutions. Related terms: Data residency, Country of origin (vendor selection). Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 15, 16, 33.

chunks.title: Data residency
chunks.text: Data residency: A requirement that data, and often the compute that processes it, stay within a named country or region. A core component of sovereign AI planning and a driver of local hosting decisions. Related terms: Sovereign AI, Direct hosting with a frontier lab. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 15, 33.

chunks.title: Country of origin (vendor selection)
chunks.text: Country of origin (vendor selection): Where an AI product or model was developed and is hosted, used as a criterion when choosing vendors. Three quarters of Deloitte's respondents weigh it; Americas firms rely far less on foreign-sourced stacks than EMEA firms. Related terms: Sovereign AI. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 5, 16.

chunks.title: Physical AI
chunks.text: Physical AI: AI systems that sense the physical world, decide and act through machines or control systems: robots, drones, autonomous vehicles, automated machinery and the digital twins that model them. Adoption leads in controlled settings such as factories and warehouses and in Asia Pacific. Related terms: Collaborative robot (cobot), Digital twin, Agentic AI. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 22, 23, 24; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 227, 229.

chunks.title: Collaborative robot (cobot)
chunks.text: Collaborative robot (cobot): An industrial robot designed to work alongside people rather than in a caged cell. Cobots were about 14 percent of industrial robot installations in 2024 and are one of the physical AI types expected to have the greatest impact. Related terms: Physical AI. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 24, 25; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 228.

chunks.title: Activation gap (access versus usage)
chunks.text: Activation gap (access versus usage): The distance between employees having sanctioned AI tools and actually using them in daily work. Deloitte found access rose by half in a year while daily use stayed flat, and names activation rather than availability as the main barrier to value. Related terms: Change management and adoption, Shadow AI, Transformation Paradox. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 8, 30; KPMG US, 2026, pages 7.

chunks.title: Pilot trap (pilot fatigue)
chunks.text: Pilot trap (pilot fatigue): The pattern in which organisations keep funding cheap, low-risk pilots instead of doing the harder work of scaling proven ones, because production needs integration, security review, compliance, monitoring and maintenance that pilots avoid. Timelines estimated at three months can stretch to eighteen. Related terms: POC-to-production gap, Micro POC. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 9; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 6, 7.

chunks.title: Pod-based structure
chunks.text: Pod-based structure: A flatter, non-hierarchical team model considered by half of large companies because AI reduces the number of roles that supervise large teams. Only a small minority had adopted it to a great extent by late 2025. Related terms: Workflow redesign. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 13.

chunks.title: AI fluency
chunks.text: AI fluency: Broad workforce literacy in using AI tools well. The most common talent response to AI (educating employees) but, on its own, far short of redesigning roles, workflows and career paths. Related terms: Upskilling and reskilling, Workflow redesign. Sources: Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 5, 14; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 14.

chunks.title: Upskilling and reskilling
chunks.text: Upskilling and reskilling: Structured programmes to raise employees' AI skills or move them into new roles. BCG's Trailblazer CEOs devote about 60 percent of AI budget to it, more than double other CEOs. Related terms: AI fluency, CEO archetypes (Followers, Pragmatists, Trailblazers). Sources: Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 26; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 14.

chunks.title: CEO archetypes (Followers, Pragmatists, Trailblazers)
chunks.text: CEO archetypes (Followers, Pragmatists, Trailblazers): BCG's clustering of CEOs by AI investment, upskilling, personal AI expertise, state of mind and confidence. About 15 percent Trailblazers invest decisively and upskill most of the workforce, about 70 percent Pragmatists invest where value is evident, and about 15 percent Followers lack conviction. Related terms: Upskilling and reskilling, Transformational budget. Sources: Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 21, 22, 23.

chunks.title: Transformational budget
chunks.text: Transformational budget: The share of an organisation's change or transformation spending allocated to AI. Trailblazer CEOs commit about three quarters of it to AI, versus about a quarter for other archetypes. Related terms: CEO archetypes (Followers, Pragmatists, Trailblazers). Sources: Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 21.

chunks.title: End-to-end AI transformation
chunks.text: End-to-end AI transformation: Reshaping whole workflows and functions with AI rather than adding AI to individual tasks. BCG frames it as the step between everyday task use and inventing new business models; McKinsey's high performers redesign workflows at three times the rate of others. Related terms: Workflow redesign, CEO archetypes (Followers, Pragmatists, Trailblazers). Sources: Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 19, 24; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 18.

chunks.title: Decision rights (for AI agents)
chunks.text: Decision rights (for AI agents): Explicit rules about which decisions an agent may take on its own and which need human approval. Governance is expected to change as agent autonomy rises; Deloitte and KPMG describe boundaries, thresholds and override triggers as the mechanism. Related terms: Human-in-the-loop (HITL), Override trigger, Unauthorised or unintended agent action. Sources: Boston Consulting Group, 2026, pages 18; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 20; KPMG US, 2026, pages 4.

chunks.title: Token-maxxing
chunks.text: Token-maxxing: Incentives that reward employees for consuming as many AI tokens as possible, sometimes tracked on internal leaderboards. Two in five large US firms would consider it; KPMG warns that usage-based incentives can reward the wrong behaviour when not tied to outcomes. Related terms: Token or usage budget, AI cost visibility. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 2, 7.

chunks.title: Token or usage budget
chunks.text: Token or usage budget: A cap on how much model usage a team, application or agent may consume, set to control AI operating cost. In place at about a third of large US firms in mid-2026; one in five organisations globally has already limited AI use because of operating costs. Related terms: FinOps, AI cost visibility, Tokenomics (AI operating cost). Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 5; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 15, 16.

chunks.title: AI cost visibility
chunks.text: AI cost visibility: The ability to see the full operating cost of AI systems, including tokens, inference, storage and compute, in real time. Only a quarter of large US firms had full visibility in mid-2026 despite most having dashboards and approval-stage cost reviews. Related terms: FinOps, Token or usage budget, Tokenomics (AI operating cost). Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 5.

chunks.title: Override trigger
chunks.text: Override trigger: A defined condition under which a person overrides an AI output: a regulatory conflict, a confidence score below a limit, a breached risk threshold, or a business judgment that differs. A third of firms still override case by case without formal criteria. Related terms: Decision rights (for AI agents), Confidence scoring, Human-in-the-loop (HITL). Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 4.

chunks.title: Chief AI Officer (CAIO)
chunks.text: Chief AI Officer (CAIO) (Chief AI Officer): A named C-suite executive accountable for AI outcomes. Accountability for AI-informed decisions is split between such named executives and the CEO or executive committee, with governance committees rarely the owner. Related terms: Decision rights (for AI agents). Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 4.

chunks.title: Pulse survey
chunks.text: Pulse survey: A short, frequently repeated survey of a fresh sample each wave. Quarter-over-quarter changes compare different respondents, so they are noisier than a panel would be. Sources: KPMG US, 2026, pages 3.

chunks.title: Application layer versus infrastructure layer
chunks.text: Application layer versus infrastructure layer: Menlo's split of generative AI spend: applications (horizontal, departmental and vertical products people use) and infrastructure (model APIs, model training and the data and orchestration layer). In 2025 the two halves were almost equal at about $19B and $18B. Related terms: Horizontal AI, Departmental AI, Vertical AI, Frontier lab. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Horizontal AI
chunks.text: Horizontal AI: General-purpose AI applications that raise productivity across all functions, such as enterprise chat copilots, agent platforms and note-taking tools. The largest and fastest-growing application category in 2025, dominated by copilots. Related terms: Application layer versus infrastructure layer, Copilot, Departmental AI. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Departmental AI
chunks.text: Departmental AI: AI applications built for a specific job role or function, such as coding, sales, customer success or HR. Coding was more than half of departmental spend in 2025. Related terms: Application layer versus infrastructure layer, Coding agent, Vertical AI. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Vertical AI
chunks.text: Vertical AI: AI applications built for a specific industry, such as healthcare, legal or government.
