Healthcare took about 43 percent of vertical spend in 2025, led by ambient clinical scribes. Related terms: Application layer versus infrastructure layer, Ambient clinical scribe, Departmental AI. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Product-led growth (PLG)
chunks.text: Product-led growth (PLG) (Product-led growth): A go-to-market motion where individual users adopt a product first and enterprise contracts follow. About a quarter of AI application spend arrives this way, four times the rate in conventional software, and near 40 percent when employee-paid tools are counted. Related terms: Shadow AI, Application layer versus infrastructure layer. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Shadow AI
chunks.text: Shadow AI: Employees using personal or unsanctioned AI tools for work, often paid for themselves and outside IT approval. Reported at more than 90 percent of companies against 40 percent with an official subscription, and a reason official tools are judged harshly. Related terms: Product-led growth (PLG), Activation gap (access versus usage), Learning gap. Sources: MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 8; Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Buy versus build
chunks.text: Buy versus build: The choice between purchasing an AI application and building on raw models in-house. Five sources converge on buying: purchased use cases rose to about three quarters, bought solutions reach production at twice the rate of internal builds, and enterprises are migrating from DIY to packaged apps. McKinsey adds a counter-current: a third have declined a software purchase because coding agents let them build it. Related terms: Coding agent, Switching cost (AI models and tools), POC-to-production gap. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 19, 20; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 9, 21.

chunks.title: Ambient clinical scribe
chunks.text: Ambient clinical scribe: An AI application that listens to clinical encounters and drafts documentation, cutting documentation time by more than half. The largest healthcare AI product category in 2025 at about $600M. Related terms: Vertical AI. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Coding agent
chunks.text: Coding agent: An AI system that plans and executes multi-step software changes, beyond line-level code completion. Coding agent spend grew from near zero to about $1.1B in 2025; about a fifth of organisations were scaling coding agents by mid-2026. Related terms: Departmental AI, Buy versus build, Agentic AI. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 3, 7.

chunks.title: Open-weight model
chunks.text: Open-weight model: A model whose weights are published for anyone to run, such as Llama, Mistral, Qwen or DeepSeek. Enterprise share of open models fell to about 11 percent by late 2025 as preference swung to closed frontier models, while startups and independent developers adopted Chinese open models quickly. Related terms: Frontier lab, Small language model. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: Context engineering
chunks.text: Context engineering: Designing what information, tools and memory a model receives for each task, as a successor to prompt engineering. Still niche in production (about 6 percent of enterprise deployments) but one of the fastest-growing skills in job postings. Related terms: Prompt engineering, RAG, Tool calling. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 207.

chunks.title: Workflow versus agent architectures
chunks.text: Workflow versus agent architectures: Menlo's taxonomy of production systems: fixed-sequence, routing-based and single-shot workflows wrap one or more model calls in predetermined logic; multi-agent, single-trajectory and multi-trajectory agents let the model plan, act, observe and adapt. Only 16 percent of enterprise deployments were true agents in late 2025. Related terms: Agentic AI, AI agent, Multi-agent orchestration. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Jevons' paradox (AI inference)
chunks.text: Jevons' paradox (AI inference): The expectation that total AI spend keeps rising even as the price per token falls, because usage volume grows faster than prices drop. Both Menlo and McKinsey use it to explain why AI is not becoming too cheap to meter. Related terms: Tokenomics (AI operating cost), Token or usage budget. Sources: Menlo Ventures, 2025; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 17.

chunks.title: Wallet share (LLM spend)
chunks.text: Wallet share (LLM spend): The share of an enterprise's model spending that goes to each vendor. a16z's Global 2000 respondents put OpenAI at a majority but shrinking, with Anthropic and Google gaining. Related terms: Multi-model strategy, Frontier lab. Sources: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: Multi-model strategy
chunks.text: Multi-model strategy: Running several model families in testing or production and routing tasks to the best one. Four in five large enterprises use three or more model families, and routing across models has largely replaced fine-tuning in enterprises. Related terms: Model routing, Wallet share (LLM spend), Fine-tuning. Sources: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026; Menlo Ventures, 2025.

chunks.title: Frontier lab
chunks.text: Frontier lab: A model developer training the most capable models, such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. Enterprise trust in labs rose sharply: about four in five now host models directly with a lab rather than only through a cloud provider. Related terms: Open-weight model, Direct hosting with a frontier lab, Wallet share (LLM spend). Sources: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026; Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 189, 190.

chunks.title: Direct hosting with a frontier lab
chunks.text: Direct hosting with a frontier lab: Consuming a model from the lab's own service rather than through a hyperscaler marketplace. Rose from about 40 percent to about 80 percent of large enterprises between March 2024 and January 2026, a signal of rising trust in labs. Related terms: Frontier lab, Data residency. Sources: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: Switching cost (AI models and tools)
chunks.text: Switching cost (AI models and tools): The effort and risk of moving from one model or tool to another once it is embedded in workflows or has learned from an organisation's data. Rising switching costs favour early footholds and learning-capable systems. Related terms: Buy versus build, Learning gap, Wallet share (LLM spend). Sources: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026; MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 18.

chunks.title: ROI multiple
chunks.text: ROI multiple: Return on AI spend expressed as a multiple of cost. In January 2026 half of large enterprises reported break-even (1x) or worse on LLM spend and 44 percent did not measure ROI precisely. Related terms: EBIT attribution to AI. Sources: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: Expert-network survey
chunks.text: Expert-network survey: A survey whose respondents are recruited from a research vendor's database by screening criteria rather than random sampling. Results can over-represent advanced adopters and are not representative of the wider market. Related terms: Pulse survey. Sources: Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), 2026.

chunks.title: GenAI Divide
chunks.text: GenAI Divide: MIT NANDA's term for the gap between the few organisations whose GenAI systems are integrated, learn from feedback and produce measurable impact, and the majority that have adopted general tools without structural change. The report's headline is that about 5 percent of custom task-specific tools reached sustained impact within six months in its sample. Related terms: Learning gap, Pilot trap (pilot fatigue), POC-to-production gap. Sources: MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 3, 6, 10.

chunks.title: Learning gap
chunks.text: Learning gap: NANDA's diagnosis of why enterprise AI tools stall: they do not retain feedback, remember context or adapt to workflows, so users reject them in favour of consumer tools. Two thirds of executives want systems that learn from feedback and retain context. Related terms: GenAI Divide, Data readiness, Shadow AI. Sources: MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 10, 12, 13, 14.

chunks.title: Prosumer (employee power user)
chunks.text: Prosumer (employee power user): A frontline employee who already uses AI heavily and can lead adoption. NANDA finds successful buyers source initiatives from such users and line managers rather than a central AI lab. Related terms: Shadow AI, Frontier Professional. Sources: MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 18, 20.

chunks.title: AI Market Disruption Index
chunks.text: AI Market Disruption Index: NANDA's 0-to-5 composite of incumbent share volatility, AI-native revenue growth, new business models, changed user behaviour and AI-driven reorganisations. Most sectors scored near zero in mid-2025; media, telecom and technology scored highest. Related terms: GenAI Divide. Sources: MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 5.

chunks.title: Agentic Web
chunks.text: Agentic Web: NANDA's forward thesis of interoperable agents on protocols such as MCP, A2A and NANDA that discover vendors, form integrations and transact across organisations. A research position from the report's authors, not a survey finding. Related terms: MCP, A2A, Agentic AI. Sources: MIT NANDA (MIT Media Lab), 2025, pages 22, 23.

chunks.title: Frontier Firm
chunks.text: Frontier Firm: Microsoft's label for organisations that learn fastest from their own AI use and encode what agents reveal into shared routines. A marketing frame that leads to Microsoft's advisory content; the underlying survey data is more reusable than the label. Related terms: Frontier Professional, Learning System (organisation). Sources: Microsoft, 2026, pages 6, 15, 21.

chunks.title: Frontier Professional
chunks.text: Frontier Professional: In Microsoft's 2026 survey, an AI user who reports advanced agent use for multi-step work, routine workflow redesign and participation in repeatable AI practices. About 16 percent of AI users; a different construct from the 19 percent 'Frontier zone' of the readiness index. Related terms: Frontier Firm, Transformation Paradox, Prosumer (employee power user). Sources: Microsoft, 2026, pages 8, 12, 23.

chunks.title: Transformation Paradox
chunks.text: Transformation Paradox: Microsoft's finding that AI users fear falling behind yet feel safer optimising current goals than redesigning work, because reinvention is rarely rewarded when results do not follow. One in ten AI users is ready but blocked by an unready organisation. Related terms: Activation gap (access versus usage), Psychological safety (AI experimentation), Frontier Professional. Sources: Microsoft, 2026, pages 12, 13.

chunks.title: Learning System (organisation)
chunks.text: Learning System (organisation): Microsoft's term for an organisation that captures, evaluates and diffuses what agents reveal about its work, with evaluation infrastructure that scales alongside agents. Organisational AI culture explained about twice as much reported AI impact as individual factors. Related terms: Frontier Firm, Evaluation-driven development. Sources: Microsoft, 2026, pages 15, 16, 19.

chunks.title: Psychological safety (AI experimentation)
chunks.text: Psychological safety (AI experimentation): Whether employees feel safe proposing new ways of working with AI and experimenting without penalty. Leaders report it far more often than employees do, and manager modelling of AI use is associated with materially higher reported AI value. Related terms: Transformation Paradox, Change management and adoption. Sources: Microsoft, 2026, pages 13.

chunks.title: Agent as managed identity
chunks.text: Agent as managed identity: Treating each AI agent like a user account with permissions, policy, lifecycle management and audit, so that unauthorised access, unintended actions and data exfiltration can be controlled. Microsoft's prescription for IT and security teams; McKinsey finds a third of organisations already mitigating unintended agent action. Related terms: Unauthorised or unintended agent action, AgentOps, RBAC. Sources: Microsoft, 2026, pages 19; McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 23.

chunks.title: AI high performer (McKinsey)
chunks.text: AI high performer (McKinsey): A respondent attributing at least 5 percent of EBIT to AI and describing AI's value as significant. About 6 percent of McKinsey's 2026 sample, unchanged from 2025; the strictest leading-group definition in this project. Related terms: EBIT attribution to AI, Workflow redesign, CEO archetypes (Followers, Pragmatists, Trailblazers). Sources: McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 17, 18.

chunks.title: Phases of AI use (experimenting, piloting, scaling)
chunks.text: Phases of AI use (experimenting, piloting, scaling): McKinsey's stages of deployment. In 2026, 44 percent of AI users were at least scaling, and large enterprises were far ahead of smaller ones on scaling agents. Related terms: POC-to-production gap, AI high performer (McKinsey). Sources: McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 5, 6.

chunks.title: EBIT attribution to AI
chunks.text: EBIT attribution to AI: A respondent's own estimate of the share of earnings before interest and tax attributable to AI. About 37 percent of organisations attribute any EBIT impact, flat year on year, while 80 percent report personal productivity gains. Related terms: AI high performer (McKinsey), ROI multiple. Sources: McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 3, 12.

chunks.title: Tokenomics (AI operating cost)
chunks.text: Tokenomics (AI operating cost): The economics of paying per token for model usage. Unit prices fall but tokens consumed rise faster, especially for agentic coding and reasoning on frontier models, so operating cost has become a design constraint that heavy users feel first. Related terms: Token or usage budget, Jevons' paradox (AI inference), AI cost visibility, FinOps. Sources: McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 15, 17, 22.

chunks.title: AI transformation office
chunks.text: AI transformation office: A central team with authority to remove bottlenecks across an AI programme. One of McKinsey's high-performer practices, though the gap to other organisations is small on this one. Related terms: Centre of Excellence (CoE), Workflow redesign. Sources: McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 19.

chunks.title: Unauthorised or unintended agent action
chunks.text: Unauthorised or unintended agent action: The risk that an autonomous agent takes an action outside its mandate, such as making a purchase, sending a message or changing a system. The first agent-specific risk measured in a major survey: a third of organisations mitigate it, 45 percent among high performers. Related terms: Decision rights (for AI agents), Agent as managed identity, Human-in-the-loop (HITL). Sources: McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 23; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 20.

chunks.title: Workflow redesign
chunks.text: Workflow redesign: Fundamentally changing how work is done around AI rather than adding AI to existing steps. The strongest single differentiator of leading organisations across sources: about 73 percent of McKinsey's high performers versus 25 percent of others, while 84 percent of Deloitte's respondents had not redesigned jobs. Related terms: End-to-end AI transformation, AI high performer (McKinsey), Pod-based structure. Sources: McKinsey & Company (QuantumBlack), 2026, pages 18, 19; Deloitte AI Institute, 2026, pages 11, 13; Microsoft, 2026, pages 6.

chunks.title: Corporate AI investment (Quid definition)
chunks.text: Corporate AI investment (Quid definition): Capital flowing into AI companies through mergers and acquisitions, minority stakes, private investment and public offerings, as tracked by Quid. Reached about $582B in 2025, of which private investment was about $345B; distinct from enterprise spend on AI products. Related terms: Application layer versus infrastructure layer. Sources: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 178, 179.

chunks.title: AI diffusion (population share)
chunks.text: AI diffusion (population share): The share of a working-age population that uses AI tools, as opposed to the share of organisations that use AI. Generative AI reached about 53 percent of US adults within three years, faster than the PC or the internet; diffusion correlates with GDP per capita. Related terms: Consumer surplus (generative AI), Shadow AI. Sources: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 199, 200, 201.

chunks.title: Consumer surplus (generative AI)
chunks.text: Consumer surplus (generative AI): The value users get from a product above what they pay, estimated from what they would need to be paid to give it up. US consumer surplus from generative AI was estimated at $172B a year in early 2026, far above producers' revenue. Related terms: AI diffusion (population share). Sources: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 192.

chunks.title: Productivity J-curve
chunks.text: Productivity J-curve: The pattern in which a general-purpose technology depresses measured productivity while firms invest in complements (skills, processes, data) and then raises it later. The AI Index cites Brynjolfsson (2026), who reads 2025 US productivity data this way: firms bear adoption costs before the larger gains show, while the macro evidence is still early and mixed. Related terms: Workflow redesign, POC-to-production gap. Sources: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 220, 221.

chunks.title: AI-exposed occupation
chunks.text: AI-exposed occupation: A job whose tasks overlap heavily with what current AI can do. Employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in the most exposed occupations fell about 16 percent relative to the least exposed by late 2025, while older cohorts grew. Related terms: Productivity J-curve. Sources: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 221, 222.

chunks.title: Automation versus augmentation
chunks.text: Automation versus augmentation: Whether an AI system completes a task on its own (automation) or works alongside a person (augmentation). In Anthropic's telemetry the two were roughly balanced through 2025, with automation briefly ahead in August; the split is one vendor's conversation mix, not a market measure. Related terms: Copilot, Agentic AI. Sources: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 202, 203.

chunks.title: Expert-public gap
chunks.text: Expert-public gap: The difference between AI experts' and the general public's expectations. In the US, 73 percent of experts but 23 percent of the public expect AI to improve how people do their jobs, and the public expects slower progress than experts in about seven of ten forecasts. Related terms: AI diffusion (population share). Sources: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI), 2026, pages 372, 374, 375.

chunks.title: Agentic era
chunks.text: Agentic era: IDC's label for a period in which AI moves from assisting people to acting autonomously across the enterprise. IDC predicts half of enterprises will use agents to redefine human-machine collaboration by 2027 and that agentic systems will be nearly half of AI spending by 2029; both are forecasts. Related terms: Agentic AI, Agentic Web. Sources: IDC, 2025.

chunks.title: Strategy and Advisory
chunks.text: Service category Strategy and Advisory: Deciding what to do and getting the organisation ready. Capabilities: Readiness and maturity assessment; Use-case identification, prioritisation and ROI modelling; Governance, responsible AI and risk frameworks; Roadmap and platform or vendor selection; Centre of Excellence and operating model design; Executive education and upskilling; Process redesign around GenAI; AI user-experience design; Change management and adoption planning. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: Data, Knowledge and Platform Foundations
chunks.text: Service category Data, Knowledge and Platform Foundations: Making enterprise data usable by AI. Capabilities: Data engineering, quality and readiness; Document intelligence pipelines (ingestion, OCR, classification, extraction, metadata); RAG architecture: chunking, hybrid search, re-ranking; Vector databases and embedding pipelines, including domain embeddings; Knowledge graphs, ontologies and semantic layers; Multimodal data pipelines; PII detection, redaction and compliance pipelines; Cloud or on-premise GenAI platform setup with security and governance. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: Model Engineering and Customisation
chunks.text: Service category Model Engineering and Customisation: Choosing, adapting and testing models. Capabilities: Model selection and cost-performance benchmarking; Proprietary model development; Prompt engineering and automated optimisation; Fine-tuning and domain adaptation (LoRA, QLoRA, RLHF, DPO); Guardrails, adversarial testing and red-teaming; Critic and evaluator agents; Multimodal model integration; Synthetic data generation; Evaluation pipelines and routing by task complexity. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 12.

chunks.title: GenAI Application and Agent Development
chunks.text: Service category GenAI Application and Agent Development: Building the copilots, assistants and agents people use. Capabilities: Enterprise copilots, knowledge assistants and conversational AI; Content generation, summarisation and document intelligence systems; Text-to-SQL, natural-language analytics and decision intelligence; Synthetic audiences and virtual personas; Agentic workflows (ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection); Memory for stateful agents; Tool calling, API orchestration and connectors; Multi-agent coordination via MCP and A2A, agent registries and marketplaces; Agent evaluation, safety and explainability; Headless system-to-system orchestration; Human-in-the-loop design and domain agents. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13.

chunks.title: Deployment and LLMOps
chunks.text: Service category Deployment and LLMOps: Running AI systems reliably, safely and affordably. Capabilities: CI/CD with prompt and model versioning; AgentOps monitoring and governance; Performance, drift and hallucination monitoring; Input validation (prompt injection, jailbreak) and output filtering; Cost and token optimisation, model routing, caching, batching; Private and on-premise LLM deployment; Multi-provider failover and disaster recovery; Security, audit logging and traceability; Serving, scaling and enterprise API integration. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13.

chunks.title: Managed Services
chunks.text: Service category Managed Services: Keeping deployed systems working and improving. Capabilities: Ongoing monitoring, prompt tuning and knowledge-base refresh; Drift detection, retraining and continuous improvement; User training, enablement and change management; KPI and business-impact tracking; SLA-driven support and governance compliance. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 13.

chunks.title: Proprietary Accelerators and Platforms
chunks.text: Service category Proprietary Accelerators and Platforms: Reusable assets a provider brings to every engagement. Capabilities: Readiness and ROI modelling tools; RAG accelerator kits and evaluation libraries; Agent orchestration platforms and prompt libraries; LLMOps and AgentOps dashboards; Cost optimisation toolkits; Governance and compliance frameworks; Domain templates and starter kits. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 14.

chunks.title: Enterprise knowledge retrieval
chunks.text: Workload Enterprise knowledge retrieval (assistive, Dominant today): Searching, extracting and reasoning over internal documents, policies, contracts and data using RAG. The first pattern most enterprises adopt and where most production deployments sit. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 15.

chunks.title: Content generation
chunks.text: Workload Content generation (assistive, Declining share): Creating, summarising, translating and transforming text. Where most organisations began; now giving way to data-grounded, higher-value work. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 15.

chunks.title: Autonomous multi-step execution
chunks.text: Workload Autonomous multi-step execution (agentic, Fastest growing): Agents that plan, reason, call tools and execute workflows across systems: claims processing, compliance review, credit analysis, analytics pipelines, backend orchestration. Maturity varies widely between vendors. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 15.

chunks.title: Domain model adaptation
chunks.text: Workload Domain model adaptation (assistive, Selective): Fine-tuning, custom embeddings, prompt optimisation and evaluation tailored to an industry. Used where domain accuracy is business-critical. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 15.

chunks.title: Multimodal processing
chunks.text: Workload Multimodal processing (assistive, Selective): Reasoning across text, images, audio and video, including OCR plus LLM pipelines and document digitisation. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 15.

chunks.title: Use cases: Financial services and banking
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Financial services and banking. Assistive and embedded: Credit memo and borrower summaries; DDQ and RFP drafting; Contract intelligence and financial spreading; Regulatory document retrieval; Fund intelligence search; Call-centre audio evaluation; Fraud detection and BI interfaces; ESG data extraction; Voice CRM note capture; Investor transcript generation. Agentic and orchestrated: Multi-step underwriting with triage and scoring; End-to-end claims auditing; Automated credit review pipelines; Collections and hardship negotiation; Sales lead qualification; Competitive intelligence monitoring; Deal analytics workflows; Model-risk validation orchestration. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 16.

chunks.title: Use cases: Healthcare and life sciences
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Healthcare and life sciences. Assistive and embedded: Clinical literature search; Medical information retrieval; Clinical trial document intelligence; Medical transcription; Patient discharge summaries; Medical copywriting; HCP sentiment analysis; Biomarker analysis; Virtual care assistants; Medical image plus text analysis. Agentic and orchestrated: Regulatory dossier automation; MLR review workflows; Pharma copilots with next-best-action; Sales forecasting pipelines; Speaker programme optimisation; Clinical trial content orchestration; Competitive intelligence monitoring; Healthcare scribe workflows. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 16.

chunks.title: Use cases: Insurance
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Insurance. Assistive and embedded: Policy Q&A; Claims document extraction; Underwriting review and pre-fill; Risk scoring from unstructured data. Agentic and orchestrated: Claims auditing with traceability; Underwriting triage and automation; Claims lifecycle risk control; Pension scheme automation. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 16.

chunks.title: Use cases: Retail and consumer goods
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Retail and consumer goods. Assistive and embedded: Product catalogue search; Customer sentiment analysis; Demand forecasting; Marketing content generation; Product image enrichment; Conversational analytics; Voice-assisted store agents. Agentic and orchestrated: Inventory optimisation; Pricing and promotion simulation; Campaign orchestration; Supply-chain risk modelling; Product matching agent suites. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 16.

chunks.title: Use cases: Manufacturing and industrial
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Manufacturing and industrial. Assistive and embedded: Bill of materials generation; Technical documentation retrieval; Product Q&A; Engineering document generation; Quality feedback analysis. Agentic and orchestrated: Root-cause analysis for yield optimisation; Purchase-order processing automation; Work-order audit agents; Product specialist agents. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 16.

chunks.title: Use cases: Energy and utilities
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Energy and utilities. Assistive and embedded: Contract search and extraction; Invoice data validation; Technical manual retrieval; Demand intelligence. Agentic and orchestrated: Invoice reconciliation workflows; Scheduler automation; Contract intelligence agents; Work-order audit automation. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 17.

chunks.title: Use cases: Telecom and technology
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Telecom and technology. Assistive and embedded: Voice-assisted recommenders; Customer-experience analytics; Product catalogue Q&A. Agentic and orchestrated: Fraud call interception agents; Call-centre orchestration with next-best-action. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 17.

chunks.title: Use cases: Legal services
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Legal services. Assistive and embedded: Demand letter drafting; Document classification; Contract clause extraction; Regulatory citation retrieval. Agentic and orchestrated: Multi-step document evaluation; Legal research orchestration with validation. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 17.

chunks.title: Use cases: Hospitality and travel
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Hospitality and travel. Assistive and embedded: Property search; Guest segmentation; Loyalty analytics. Agentic and orchestrated: Multi-agent proposal generation; Personalised property recommendations. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 17.

chunks.title: Use cases: Automotive and mobility
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Automotive and mobility. Assistive and embedded: Vehicle document processing; Immigration and tax document extraction. Agentic and orchestrated: Procurement agents; Immigration and tax workflow automation; Supplier assessment workflows. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 17.

chunks.title: Use cases: Public sector and government
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Public sector and government. Assistive and embedded: Document digitisation; Citizen chatbots; Policy retrieval; Political narrative analysis. Agentic and orchestrated: Workflow modernisation; Crime prediction platforms; Social listening with reasoning. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 17.

chunks.title: Use cases: Media, publishing and education
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Media, publishing and education. Assistive and embedded: Alt-text generation; Editorial tagging; Academic Q&A assistants; Peer-review support; Content summarisation; Scientific image description. Agentic and orchestrated: Course content orchestration; Academic Q&A with verification; Audience segmentation platforms. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 17.

chunks.title: Use cases: Cross-industry (horizontal)
chunks.text: GenAI use cases in Cross-industry (horizontal). Assistive and embedded: HR and legal Q&A; Internal knowledge search; Code migration assistants; Executive reporting; Conversational BI; Marketing analytics; Employee onboarding; Email summarisation; KPI chatbots; Workforce analytics. Agentic and orchestrated: IT issue-resolution agents; HR process automation; Competitive intelligence monitoring; Data engineering agents; RFP evaluation; Invoice reconciliation; DevOps automation; Project planning agents; Recruitment screening; Procurement orchestration. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 18.

chunks.title: Project-based
chunks.text: Engagement model Project-based (Fixed scope or time and materials): Dominant entry point for POCs and early production. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 22.

chunks.title: Capacity-led scaling
chunks.text: Engagement model Capacity-led scaling (Dedicated pods, staff augmentation): Widely used as programmes expand, especially multi-use-case pipelines. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 22.

chunks.title: Run and operate
chunks.text: Engagement model Run and operate (Managed services): Fastest growing, driven by rising production deployments. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 22.

chunks.title: Outcome-linked
chunks.text: Engagement model Outcome-linked (Outcome or value-based fees): Selective but rising; used in mature, KPI-driven deployments. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 22.

chunks.title: Platform or subscription
chunks.text: Engagement model Platform or subscription (Licence or subscription): Emerging, mainly among platform-led or IP-driven vendors. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 22.

chunks.title: Co-innovation
chunks.text: Engagement model Co-innovation (Joint development): Used for strategic or complex initiatives. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 22.

chunks.title: Cost and compute optimisation
chunks.text: Practice area Cost and compute optimisation: Right-sized model selection and multi-model routing; RAG-first design to reduce token use; Prompt compression, caching and batching; Auto-scaling and workload-aware compute. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20.

chunks.title: Token efficiency and performance
chunks.text: Practice area Token efficiency and performance: Context pruning, chunking and hybrid retrieval; Structured prompts and output control; Asynchronous and parallel agent workflows; Latency, throughput and quality monitoring. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20.

chunks.title: Monitoring and LLMOps
chunks.text: Practice area Monitoring and LLMOps: Real-time tracking of tokens, cost, latency and accuracy; Drift and hallucination tracking with feedback loops; A/B testing, versioning and controlled releases; End-to-end observability. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20.

chunks.title: Governance and risk management
chunks.text: Practice area Governance and risk management: Responsible-AI guardrails for bias, hallucination and explainability; Human-in-the-loop validation for critical decisions; Version control for models, prompts and workflows; Audit trails and traceability. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20.

chunks.title: Security and compliance
chunks.text: Practice area Security and compliance: Role-based access control and encryption; PII detection, masking and secure data handling; Private cloud or VPC deployment and secure APIs; SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA and industry standards. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20.

chunks.title: Value and operationalisation
chunks.text: Practice area Value and operationalisation: KPI-driven tracking of cost, accuracy and productivity; Reusable accelerators, CoEs and standard frameworks; Continuous optimisation from usage insight; Transition from experimentation to enterprise-grade AI. Sources: AIM Research (AIM Media House LLC), 2026, pages 20.

chunks.title: Maturity tier: Emerging
chunks.text: IDC real-time data maturity tier Emerging: Bottom 30 percent of respondents, 30 percent of the sample (n = 188), average composite score 35 out of 100. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 7, 8.

chunks.title: Maturity tier: Developing
chunks.text: IDC real-time data maturity tier Developing: 30th to 60th of respondents, 31 percent of the sample (n = 195), average composite score 50 out of 100. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 7, 8.

chunks.title: Maturity tier: Advanced
chunks.text: IDC real-time data maturity tier Advanced: 60th to 80th of respondents, 19 percent of the sample (n = 117), average composite score 60 out of 100. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 7, 8.

chunks.title: Maturity tier: Leaders
chunks.text: IDC real-time data maturity tier Leaders: Top 20 percent of respondents, 20 percent of the sample (n = 123), average composite score 74 out of 100. Sources: IDC Custom Solutions, 2026, pages 7, 8.
